subtopic: STATEMENT BY ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE OF EXPENDITURE IN CONNECTION THEREWITH.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. A. K. MACLEAN (Acting Minister of Finance):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE OF EXPENDITURE IN CONNECTION THEREWITH.
speechtext:
Yesterday the leader of the Opposition made inquiry concerning a return asked for on 20th March last in reference to the expenses in connection with the last Victory Loan. As he evidently desires that this information be submitted prior to the introduction of the War Appropriation Bill, I ask the leave of'the House to make a statement wdiich I hope will give him the information he desires. The reason the return has not been brought down was that full statements of all expenses in connection with the loan are not available to the department; consequently it is not possible to give to the House the exact information required by the Order referred to. However, I hope to be able to give the House substantially the information asked for, so that the progress of the War Appropriation Bill may not be delayed.
All expenditure in the way of remuneration for services in connection with the loan may be divided into three classes: first, remuneration to co-operating bond dealers and brokers; second, commission to canvassers; third, remuneration to banks.
As to the first, remuneration to co-operating bond dealers and brokers, in this loan the principle of co-operation rather

than competition among . brokers was adopted in order to organize and cover the whole country as effectively as possible. For this work practically the whole organization of all bond dealers and brokers was employed. The arrangement made by the Minister of Finance in reference to the remuneration of these firms was that at the close of the loan, after consultation with the Dominion Executive Committee and the consideration of any views or recommendations put forward by them, the amount to be paid would be based on t'he value of the services rendered in connection with the campaign by the several bond dealers and brokers. Some adjustments may yet have to be made, bat on April 5th the total payment under this head was approximately $750,000. Additional payments may yet have to be made to brokers. On the other hand, only last *week $30,000 was refunded by three of the principal bond houses of Toronto, and a few days ago $2,000 was refunded by the chairman of the chief committee in Saskatchewan. Possibly further refunds may be made of allowances paid to several of the committees throughout the Dominion.
As to commissions to canvassers, I may say that local canvassers were employed to solicit subscriptions and were given certain territory or lists of prospective subscribers to cover. Local canvassers were not permitted to solicit subscriptions .from those who. had been placed upon the special subscriptions list, which composed all prospective subscribers who, under previous loans, had subscribed for bonds to the amount of $25,000 or over. That is, any persons receiving subscriptions from those who had subscribed for sums of $25,000 or over in previous loans were to receive no commission thereon. Arrangements for the canvassing for subscriptions from these were made by the Special Subscriptions Committee, and no commissions were paid upon the same.
The Dominion Executive Committee was authorized to pay commissions to local canvassers on the following basis:
(a)	In all places having a population of more than 10,000, local canvassers were to be paid a commission of i Of 1 per cent upon all subscriptions obtained by them.
(b)	In places having a population of less than 10,000 and in rural sections, canvassers. were to be paid one-half of one per cent on all subscriptions obtained in their respective sections, whether secured by the canvassers or placed by subscribers directly with the banks, excluding, of
course, subscriptions from the Special List referred to above.
As of April 5, total disbursements for commissions to canvassers were $1,140,813.75.
As to remuneration to banks, a remuneration to chartered banks of one-quarter of one per cent on' the total allotment was paid for receiving subscriptions, payments, delivering interim certificates and definite bonds, and cashing coupons during the term of the loan-that is, during the 5, 10 or 20-year loan periods, as the case might be. The total amount paid to the banks for this purpose was $984,395.64. The allotment of the loan reaching $398,000,000 consisted of 5, 10 and 20-year bonds bearing 5i per cent interest. The issue was made at par with the privilege of deferred payments. It is estimated that the total expenses will reach approximately li per cent of the amount allotted.	[DOT]
Putting the matter in concise form, the expenses of the loan up to date have been as follows:
Organization expenses	 $ 376,000
For Publicity Campaign,
(a)	Through the Dominion Publicity Committee	 163,000
(b)	Through Canadian Press Association (disbursements to date) 207,000
For remuneration to Brokers and
Bond Dealers	 750,000
Commissions to canvassers	 1,140,000
Remuneration to Banks	 984,395
Total	 $3,620,395
In addition to this, there are, of course, the departmental expenses for printing the interim receipts, for engraving the bonds, for the staff employed, numbering some 700 persons, in the Department of Finance, who have been specially engaged upon this work since last December. It is estimated that the total cost of the loan, when finally available, will approximate $5,000,000, or about one and one-quarter per cent of the whole loan, which I think may be regarded by everybody as a very satisfactory rate.
The price of the securities issued was, of course, par, but by acceleration of payments, a slight discount, equal to the rate of interest which the bonds bear, namely, 5J per cent, was allowed to subscribers. Perhaps I may make that clearer to the House by saying that if a subscriber paid his subscription in full on January 2, last, he would pay for his bonds at the rate of 99 -107; if he paid in full on February 1, last, he would pay at the rate of 99 -467; if he paid on March 1, he would pay at the rate of 99-722; if he paid on April 1, he would pay at the rate of 99-909, and if he deferred his payment in full until the 1st

of May, as *he might do, he would pay at the rate of 100 per cent. I trust this will give to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and to the House, the information desired. I shall pass over to my right hon. friend the statement from which I have read, and if there is any other information which he desires and which I can possibly give to him, I shall he glad to do so. But I trust that, with the information I have given, he will inform the Prime Minister that he may proceed with the War Appropriation Bill.

On motion of Horn Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior) Bill No. 39, to amend the Yukon Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-"Section 115, abolition of Council and new Council provided for."

Is the Governor in Council, in regard to the selections to be made, to confine its choice to judicial officers, or are the selections to be made generally of persons presumed to be capable of performing the duties attaching to the council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not sure that I understand the hon. gentleman's question, but the Yukon Act provides that there shall be appointed a commissioner and also that there ishall be an administrator,~ whose duties shall be to substitute for the commissioner in the absence or illness of the latter. Without power being given under the Act to abolish those offices, they cannot be abolished. They are, however, already abolished under the War Measures Act, but it is the intention that this legislation shall confirm the action taken, and that it shall date back so as to ratify that action. There are, in the general administrative machinery of the Yukon, other offices which have been abolished as well, and notifications have gone to all the holders of those offices that their services shall cease on the 30th of April, but the Act doeis not provide for the creation of those offices, and consequently it does not need to be amended in so far as those "offices are concerned.
The Bill does not apply to the last class of officers?

On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (Minister of Railways), the House went into committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide that the receipts and revenues of the Canadian Government railways and of any railway under the charge, management or direction of the Minister may be deposited in a Suspense Account, and the working expenses of the said railways may be defrayed therefrom, and in the event of a deficit occurring at any time, the amount of such deficit shall be payable out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, and in the event of a surplus the amount thereof may be transferred to the said Fund; the Suspense Account and all payments therefrom being subject to the audit of the Auditor General of Canada.

I wish to move that the resolution be, amended to read as follows:
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide that the working expenses of the Canadian Government railways and of any railway under the charge, management or direction of the Minister of Railways and Canals shall be paid out of the receipts and revenues of the said railway, and in the event of a deficit occurring at any time during any fiscal year the amount of such deficit shall be payable out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, the said deficit to be voted by Parliament at its first session following the close of suoh fiscal year.
This change is made at the suggestion of the Auditor General, and is for the purpose of giving Parliament control in case there is a deficit.

I think this resolution is open to one objection. When I first read the resolution I was favourably impressed with it as a businesslike arrangement, but on further consideration the impression I have is that it will withdraw a very important matter of public business from the consideration of Parliament, lit proposes to set apart a portion of the Government business and say that that shall not be managed as other Government business, but shall be treated as a separate account. It might be argued with some force by the minister that putting this annual appropriation in the estimates swells the total, and that it is, after all, a mere matter of book-keeping. The Government railways on the whole will probably pay their expenses, but in many years they have not, although we are all hoping for better things. It is only in the event of. a deficit occurring that

Parliament would be asked to vote the money, but in the event of there being do deficit the consideration of the railway situation would probably be withdrawn from the consideration of Parliament. I hope the minister will give the matter further consideration. Perhaps, the view I take of it is1 not correct, but it seems to me, where the appropriations for the railway will run into so many million dollars, that there ie no good reason why Parliament should not have the opportunity every year of considering the appropriations, and that would necessarily open the way for a general criticism and inquiry, which, after all, is one of the chief purposes for which Parliament is assembled. There may be another side to this question, but fOT the moment I ask the Acting Minister of Finance whether he is- not, as a mere matter of convenience-and it would be no doubt a convenience to the department-taking aw-ay from Parliament one of its most valuable and important duties.

The principle
which the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) enunciates would no doubt be a sound one if it bad reference to taxation. Beyond doubt Parliament should possess of itself the sole right of appropriating any moneys collected from the people of this country by means of taxation, but I submit that the revenues which are obtained by the Government railways of Canada from the people of Canada, for services rendered by that railway, are in a different position altogether from revenues received by wray of taxation. I think a fair test of the fairness of the proposal contained in the resolution is this: Does the continuance of the practice of voting a general amount in the estimates after all mean anything? Last year I think we were asked to vote a sum of about thirty-five millions under the heading "Operating Expenses of the Government Bailway Systems of Canada." That, of course, gives no particular information to Parliament. No questions, therefore, are ever asked under that item. The amount cannot be approximated by the Department of Railways with any accuracy whatever. I am told by the officers of the department that this year they cannot estimate within five to ten million dollars what would be the operating expenses of the Canadian Government Railway system during the present fiscal year. My objection to the inclusion of the amount in the annual estimates is that it swells our general estimates unduly/ and no good purpose is served by it.
What harm is done?

It leaves the impression abroad tbat our annual expenditure as shown to be in the estimates is greater than it actually is. I think it is only a fair proposal that the revenues of *a railway system should be used to pay operating expenses, without Parliament being asked to vote that amount. If the amount could be voted with any degree of accuracy, possibly some good might come ou't of it, but it has never in the past interested the House, and I say it is unfair to the railway system. It is unfair to the estimates to load them with this amount. The Canadian Government are to-day the owners of the Canadian Northern railway system. *
And they do not operate it.

Our operating expenses will not be voted, in this manner. They were not voted this way last year. We voted a certain amount to take care of the deficit. We shall ask Parliament to do the same thing this session. If the resolution is adopted by the House, I think the financial position of the Intercolonial will really be presented to Parliament, in a better form than heretofore. If there is a deficit Parliament will be asked to vote that deficit, and a very definite and clear cut discussion may then take place upon, the administration of the railroad, because Parliament is asked to vote a deficit which it has never been asked to do before. The principle is not a new one. The Intercolonial has what they call a store account. The minister is permitted to. provide a certain sum for the purchase of railway supplies and material, and while there is a limitation of 81,500,000 to that account, still the principle is exactly the same. The same principle applies to the King's Printer.

We increased
the store account to 16,000,000 last night.
Mr. .A. K. MACLEAN:	The principle
is just the same, and it applies to the King's Printer. The principle in the Bill is this:	that the Government railway system ,be permitted to pay, out of its own revenue, its operating expenses. I submit that is a fair proposal, and I hope it will be accepted by the committee.
Suppose it is a surplus?

Do not suppose
that
We must suppose all kind of things now.

The book-keeping system is not interfered with. Every dollar and every cent that goes to the system are credited to the Receiver General. Every cent paid out -by the railway is paid by cheque at Moncton upon the Bank of Montreal, Ottawa, where the Government account is kept.

I am glad to hear the
Minister of Finance state to-day that we have the Canadian Northern, because last night apparently we had lost it.

It is 'a hide-and-seek
game.

The Minister of Railways yesterday proposed a new resolution to increase the amount that might be voted for stores to $6,000,000. He told us the increase was required on accouht of the Transcontinental and International roads but he did not mention the Canadian Northern, and I inferred from that that he figured the Government did not at the present lime own the Canadian Northern. I am further strengthened in that opinion by the fact that the Government solicitor in Toronto two or three days ago made the statement -before the commission that he could not get a report of the earnings of the Canadian Northern Railway company since last October. Now, if we own the road, surely we should be able to get a statement of its earnings.
I might say to the hon. gentleman that the statements were given to the solicitor immediately.

Why did he have to go to the Commission and as-k for the statement? He said he could not get it from the proper sources. I know he got the statement the next day. Of course, he would have to get it; that is quite natural, but he could not get it up to that time. The hon. Minister of Finance states he does not want to have his estimates loaded up with a deficit. I do not think there is any question, if the railways of this country are managed by the Government as they have been, that we may forget about surpluses. It will be a question of deficits, and we want honest bookkeeping in this country. If we are making a loss on the railway, let us know it and show where we stand, and not try to cover it up by adopting some other system. If we are making a loss, it is a loss to Canada, and increasing Canada's debt, and why not show it,
as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) suggests?
Do I understand my hon. friend to say he is in favour of the resolution?
No, he is against it.
The resolution proposes to accomplish just what my hon. friend says he would like to see.
In what way?
Inasmuch as the deficits-and he says we will always have a deficit-will be disclosed in the estimates because it must then be voted. Is my hon. friend supporting the resolution?
No, he is against it.
I do not understand that he is against it. I do not know wrhat he means.
He wants Parliament to control public funds. .

Parliament is not dispossessing itself of the control of anything. I understand him to say, in his judgment, the operation of railways in Canada fey the Government will always result in a deficit, and he would like to have these deficits put flearly before Parliament. Did I understand the hon. gentleman correctly? If I understood his statement rightly, this resolution, being enacted into the form of a Bill, will accomplish exactly what he wants. It has hardly been possible heretofore to know what was the actual result of the operation of the Canadian Government Railway system in Canada unless one took the trouble to go through the annual report. The Government has no desire to hide anything. I think that the Minister of Railways and Canals is perfectly justified in asking to be allowed to administer the Government Railway system in the same manner as other railways are administered.
Does not the resolution state that any unappropriated fund shall be drawn upon to the extent of the deficit?

Perhaps my hon. friend did not hear the amendment proposed, and perhaps I was wrong in pressing my question because he had the original resolution before him. The amended resolution will read:
That It is expedient to provide that the working expenses of the Canadian Government Railways and of any railway under the charge and management or direction of the Minister of Railways and Canals shall be-

What does my hon. friend mean by " andof any railway under the charge and management or direction of the Minister of Railways and Canals?" Has he anything in his mind? Does that mean the Canadian Northern?
No. I think it was intended to cover the Transcontinental railway.
That is part of the Canadian Government Railway system, is it not?
I am not sure as to that.
Oh.
I do not see why my statement should occasion any merriment on the part of any hon. gentlemen opposite. If any hon. gentlemen knows what it means they might stand up and inform the House.
We will let the Government do that.

The words " Canadian Government railways " might be limited by statute to what is known as the Intercolonial railway and the Prince Edward Island railway. If they are limited to those railways then I am perfectly right in my statement and hon. gentlemen are wrong in their laughter.
Are they so limited?
The question is whether all the railways owned by the Canadian Government are Canadian Government railways or whether the words are limited by the statute to the railways mentioned by my hon. friend.

Possibly my hon. friend is right, but there need not be any discussion about the words "and of any railway under the charge and management or direction of the Minister of Railways and Canals," because that can be amended later. Let me read the amendment:
That it is' expedient to provide that the working expenses of the Canadian Government Railways and of any railway under the charge and management or direction of the Minister .of Railways and Canals shall .he paid out of the receipts and revenues of the said railways, and in the event of a deficit occurring at any time during any fiscal year, the amount of such deficit shall be -payable out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, the said deficit to be voted by Parliament at its first session following the close of such fiscal year.

Touching the question of the interpretation of the expression "Canadian Government railways," the Acting Minister of Finance is perhaps unaware that his colleague, the "Minister of Railways and Canals, last night gave his own interpretation-and I am not objecting to it-that "Canadian Government railways" includes the Transcontinental and all other Government railways except the Canadian Northern. On the faith of that interpretation we allowed the hon. gentleman to increase his stores account from $1,500,000 to $6,000,000. I am merely asking whether the hon. gentleman has anything particularly in his mind. I appreciate the point made by the Acting Minister of Finance as to the distinction between revenue which represents taxation and revenue qf different kinds. But his argument will probably carry him a little farther than he appreciates when we come to apply it. If the principle of the resolution is sound, why not apply it to other departments as well? Suppose I were to suggest that we should apply it to the Department of Customs, my hon. friend would say at once:	"That is taxation."
So it is. But, suppose we should go to the Post Office Department. That is not taxation. The postage stamp represents payment for service just as much as the railway ticket represents payment for service. If my hon. friend's argument is good that this is a proper thing to do with regard to Government railways, the same argument might be advanced with regard to the Post Office Department. You might extend that in different directions. What it really means is that the appropriation for each railway system which has hitherto always been made by parliament is no longer to be made by Parliament and whatever opportunities the making of the appropriation offered for enquiry and discussion and criticism will not longer be available. The annual appropriation of the moneys needed for the operation of the Intercolonial railway has always presented an opportunity for widespread inquiry, criticism and discussion. The withdrawing of that appropriation from Parliament, I grant you, as a mere matter of book-keeping, may not make any difference, but at the same time I think there is no good reason why Parliament should give up the privilege of making the annual vote for a mere matter of book-keeping. I do not see that it is going to make one cent's worth of difference to the treasury of Canada one way or the other, but as a pure matter of parlia-

mentary procedure we should keep as far as possible to .the principle of parliamentary control.

In reference to
the case suggested by the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) of the Post Office I would submit that it is hardly analogous. The Government Railway system is a well, defined and limited operation. It is administered from a single office at Moncton. I imagine that all the revenues of the road go there first and ultimately to Ottawa. All operating expenses are incurred at that point. In the case of the post office system, there must be twenty thousand or thirty thousand (branches throughout Canada extending from coast to coast.

There are railway stations all over Canada.
Mr. A. K. MA'OLEAN: I fail to see how in any respect the cases are analogous. The money is received by the post office but there are scores and scores of offices receiving that revenue. You could hardly pay the operating expenses of the post office in Vancouver .out of the revenues received, at, say, St. John, N.B. In the case of the railway system the revenues all go into the head office of the system at Moncton and from there all expenditures are authorized, all operating expenses are paid and there is established the Government Railway audit system. The Government Railway accounts are audited at Moncton.
Reverting to the question asked by my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), will any of the working expenses of the Canadian Northern railway come under this resolution?

What is the
objection-to that?

There is no objection at all, but it loads up the estimates with an amount that really should not be there. But there is no desire in any way, shape or form, so far as the Railway Department and the Finance Department are concerned, to change, the method of carrying on the expenditures in connection with the Canadian Government Railway system.
It is simply a blind.

It is not a blind. I do not see how the right hon. gentleman can make such a statement. We may have to pay out probably a larger amount than we estimate at the present time, for this reason: You cannot tell at the present time how things are going to turn out, as regards the cost of labour, and so on, and it may probably involve adding a considerable amount more than was at first thought necessary in order to carry on the operations of the Government system.
Supposing we do. The leader of the Opposition was right; it is a blind.
Will this mean an increase of the staff?
It does not involve increasing the staff in any respect. It is simply a matter of book-keeping and the money will be deposited and paid out in exactly the same manner as before.

We do not
want to be accused of indulging in captious criticism, because, we desire to facilitate the despatch of business, but the Minister of Railways has told us that he does not want this money to appear in the esti-

mates.. If that is not a blind, what is it?
( By all means let us have the truth.

As far as having the
truth is 'concerned, I am trying to explain to the right lion, gentleman, as clearly as I cam, what is .proposed. Now, what is the present system? The revenues are deposited to the credit of the Receiver General, and the cheques are issued by the railway and passed) toy the Auditor General at Ottawa. That system will still continue in exactly the same manner.
No.

There is no question
about it.
Will there be the same method of treating the revenues of the railway?
Just the same as before.

No; because
at the present time the' revenues of the road, like the revenue of the post office, are sent to Ottawa and put in the consolidated revenue fund, but what my hon. friend proposes is collect the revenues of the Government railways and send them to Moncton and expend them there.

If the right hon. gentleman has gathered that- meaning from anything that I have said, he has gathered an erroneous impression. The financial representative of the Department of Railways and Canals tells me that there will be no change of the kind at all; the money will be deposited in exactly the same manner as before, and the expenditures will toe made in the same way. On the motion of Hon. A. K. MACLEAN, acting Minister of Finance, the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to consolidate, revise and amend the Civil Service Act of Canada; and to provide that the salary of the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission shall be six thousand dollars per annum; and to make provision for the readjustment of grades and salaries in the various classes of the Inside Service, and for the preparation by the Commission of schedules of the positions, duties, and salaries of the Outside Service or of any portion or branch thereof; and to make appointments to the public service upon competitive examination and otherwise eliminate political patronage in the control and management of the said service.

I hope it may be satisfactory to the committee to discuss this matter after the. introduction of the Bill. Primarily, the purpose of introducing this resolution is to amend the Civil Service Act in order to provide that in so far as possible all regulations and statutory requirements that are to-day applicable to the Inside Service shall apply to the Outside Service. Appointments to what is called the Outside Service shall hereafter be made by the Civil Service Commission and upon the basis of competitive examination.

An Order in Council was passed on the 13th day of February last upon this subject, and I assume that hon. gentlemen know the general tenor of that Order in Council. It appeared quite fully in the press of the country at the time, but, perhaps, it might be quite proper that I should just in a few words give the purport of it. That Order in Council provided that where knowledge of a professional or technical character was required on the part of any person about to be appointed to the public service the appointment should be made by the deputy head and the Civil Service Commission instead of by the Governor General in Council on the recommendation of the deputy head as heretofore. The Order in Council also provided that the Civil Service Commission should, in so far as possible, make appointments to the Outside Service by competitive examination. It required all officers, clerks, and employees in the Outside Service to be appointed in the same manner as persons were appointed to the Inside Service, viz., after competitive examination. The Order in Council also provided that temporary employment in the Outside Service should be authorized from time to time as the Commission deemed necessary and the Commission were also authorized to determine the purpose for which the employment was authorized, and that it should be mentioned in the certificate of qualification to be issued by the Commission.
It also provided that promotions in the Civil Service should be made for merit upon the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission and of the deputy head of the department. It also provided that no trans-. fer should be made from the Outside Service to the Inside Service under the provisions of Section 50 of the Civil Service Act unless the person concerned obtained from the Civil Service Commission a certificate. The Order in Council also provided that in all competitive examinations held under the Civil Service Act, persons who had been on active service overseas in the military or naval forces of His Majesty, or of any allies of His Majesty, and who had left such service with an honourable record, or who had been honourably discharged, and obtained sufficient marks to pass the required examination should, irrespective of the marks they obtained, be placed in the order of merit on the list of successful candidates above all other candidates. In a general way this is the purport of the Order in Council, which was more in the nature of a direction to the Civi' Service Commission than otherwise. There will be other changes, but if the 'Committee will be satisfied with these explanations of the Order in Council, ample time will be given after the Bill is printed and distributed to enable members to become acquainted with its provisions. That had reference to the matter of appointments to the railway service. I do not wish to unduly criticise the acting Minister of Finance;
I think, from what I heard of him and from him when he sat on this side of the House, that he is acting in good faith and means well. He says that if the right hon. present leader of the Opposition had been returned to power he might not have been able to carry out such a reform as this. Well, one thing I appreciate in public life is sincerity and frankness. When the right hon. gentleman was Prime Minister-in the elections of 1908-he promised one great reform, a reform of the Inside Civil Service. Shortly afterwards, he passed a law which is on the statute book to-day, the Civil Service Act. The resolution was introduced by Hon. Mr. Fisher, then Minister of Agriculture, and in it there was laid down for the first time in Canada the principle of competitive examination, a principle which has been accepted in England
['Mr. A. K. Maclean.]
and which has made the English Civil Service the best in the world. Moreover, that principle was lived up to by the Liberal Administration which went out of office in 1911. I am not so sure that my hon. friend will find comfort in the record of his associates -as 'regards the operation of the Civil Service Act. It was put to a very severe test by those who came into office in 1911. So much so, indeed, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), speaking of the system of patronage said:
It almost always causes the dry rot and disintegration that break up 'Government after Government and party after party. .	. .If
[DOT]there is any canker of public corruption, in 99 cases out of 100 you can trace it to the baneful effect of political party patronage.
My hon. friend used those strong words after he had seen his own colleagues in the late Government administering the Civil Service Act. He had seen what Mr. Rogers, the late Minister of Public Works, had done in his own department, namely, appointing in defiance of the Civil Service Commission, a gentleman as chief architect of the Public Works Department, giving him a salary of $7,000, after the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission had refused to recommend him as chief architect, and also had refused to yield to the ultimatum that had been served upon him to recommend such a high salary for that official. I am glad that the Minister of Public Works of to-day has given a permanent leave of absence to that official. My hon. friend may, therefore, just as well have more faith in his old friends than in his new associates as regards the milennium which he is seeking to bring about by this legislation. Does he not know that in 1904, in 1908, and in 1911 promises of Civil Service reform were made by members of the Conservative party, and that Sir Robert Borden pledged himself that there would be Civil Service reform not only in the Inside Service, but in the Outside Service? In the month of December last the Government issued a new manifesto, in which a solemn pledge was taken before the electors of Canada that this Government would- put an end for the future to patronage in the public service. At that time, however, and during several weeks afterwards, hundreds of young men and young girls were being taken into the various Government boards and departments, always under the shallow pretext of winning the war. In the city of Ottawa, although we had another solemn pledge embalmed in -an Order in Council, passed in 1915, that preference would always be given returned soldiers, we found that the best

positions in the Civil -Service were given, not to returned soldiers, but to party managers and ward politicians. Take the case of the postmastership at Ottawa. In the first place, I do not know why Mr. Gouin, the postmaster, was relieved of his duties. Hie was still .hale and hearty, a splendid official, giving entire satisfaction to the pulblie. Nevertheless, he was superannuated, and to the dismay of the .people, Mr. Acres, who wars the secretary of the 'Conservative association in Ottawa, was given the position, in defiance of the protest of the Civil Sendee Federation. The Civil Service 'Federation, iwhioh, I believe, has been consulted concerning this Rill, protested most vehemently to the Prime Minister when it became known that Mk. Acres would fee appointed, ibeoau.se (there were able officials of (twenty and twenity-five years' standing in the Ottawa post office whose Services were ignored. And for what purpose? To give a fat office t-o the secretary of the Ottawa Conservative association. I do not know Mr. Acres. I hope he will prove a good official. 1 know he is a respected citizen of the city of Ottawa. But why did the Government pass over the heads of old employees in the Ottawa post office, after the .pledge had (been given toy the Prime Minister and by some of his colleagues at the beginning of 'the election (campaign, that there would be no more patronage in the public service.
Let ius take the case of the Montreal customs oollectorshiip. I know Mr. Weldon, who will prove an excellent collector of customs. Ait the last session of Parliament, when we were discussing the estimates, the present Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) made a distinct promise that this office would go to a returned soldier. Yet, a few months after that solemn pledge was given, alderman Weldon was given the position. T do not object to Mr. Weldon personally. I know he will be an excellent collector of customs, I know he has served in South Africa. The fact remains, however, that a pledge was given that a returned soldier would .get the Montreal colleotorship of customs. There again 'the principle of promotion, the prin-iciple of competition, was not (followed. Quite a host of other appointments from the ranks of the friends of the patty have been made. An appointment was given ,to Mr. Nichols, half brother of the present Minister of Finance. Mr. Bratoazon a former member of this House was appointed Superintendent of Works on the Ottawa
river. I forget the others, bub quite an array of Conservative politicians received fat appointments immediately before or immediately after the election, although at that time the Government was preaching throughout the land that there would toe no more patronage at Ottawa. In the case of an appointment made at Wingham, Ontario, the principle that postmasters should be appointed only by the Civil Service Commission was again made light of, and a member of the local, legislature, I forget his name, was appointed postmaster. The Acting Minister of Finance should not be surprised if we are a little dubious as to the sincerity of the Government in regard to this proposed reform. Until we have strong evidence of its sincerity, we are-"Doubting- Thomases." We shall, at all events, await with interest the explanation of the Government in regard to the appointment of Mr. Acres at Ottawa. I am anxious to hear what the Acting Minister of Finance has to say about that.

A few moments
age I stated that I did not think the great advance proposed by the terms of the Order in Council in the Civil Service of this country could have been accomplished 'by the leader of the Opposition, if he were in power as leader of the Liberal party, nor by the present Prime Minister if he were in office as head of the Conservative party. I did not intend to' detract in the slightest from the credit due to the ministry led by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition for passing the Civil Service Act of 1908. On the contrary, I think that ministry is entitled to every possible credit for passing that Act. 'It was a great reform. I repeat I do not in the slightest degree wish to minimize the efforts made by the ministry of that day. because I was in Parliament myself and supported the Bill.
The Inside Service is very small 'as compared with the Outside 'Service in Canada, and the reform contemplated by the Bill which I am about to introduce was only possible by reason of the political conditions which now exist. When my hon. friend referred to the late ministry I think he meant the ministry of which he was a member himself, because the late ministry was the ministry led by the present Prime Minister and was supported by what was known' as the Conservative party. My hon. friend is inclined to doubt whether the Act to be framed on the lines indicated by me a few moments ago will be faithfully administered and strictly adhered to. It is very natural for my hon.

friends opposite to have doubts ae to the ability of a ministry to enforce the promised reform in respect to the Civil Service, and I do not blame them in the slightest degree for expressing this doubt. It might well have been expressed by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House and by the citizens of Canada. It is such a tremendous reform to undertake that any attempt in that direction by the Government deserves the sympathy and support of every hon. gentleman in this House, no matter on which side of the Speaker he sits, because that reform can only be accomplished by having the intelligent support of the people of this country. To apply the provisions of the Civil Service Act to the Outside Service was what all parties and all governments in the past have baulked at and refused to do. But the present ministry are attempting to carry out faithfully (and strictly the declaration which. was made to the country by the right hon. the Prime Minister some time prior to the last election.
I do not think it is fair to judge of the bona tides of the Government in this matter by appointments which were made prior to the passage of the Order in Council. As regards appointments at Ottawa and Montreal, my hon, friend the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) says 'that in each case the men appointed were excellent in every respect. I take -it that he means that both Mr. Acres and Mr. Weldon will make capable and efficient public servants. If that be so, I doubt if the public are very much interested as to which party both or either of these gentleman supported.
Except that the principle of promotion was ignored.

At that time the principle of promotion in the Outside Service had not been fully worked out, and no Order in Council had been promulgated. My hon. friend must remember that the elections took place only on the 17th December.
We remember.

And polling overseas was not concluded until the 18th day of January this year. Some time early in February the Order in Council was promulgated. I do not think -my hon. friend from Maisonneuve will impress any body in this country very strongly when he urges as a criticism of the Bill which is to be introduced, or of the proposed policy of the Government, the fact that it has happened that one or two former Conservatives were

appointed to office before the passage of this Order in Council. I have no doubt that before this Order in Council was passed, some persons wTere appointed to office, who w'ere Liberals.
Mr, LEMIEUX: There was a stampede.

I do not know what my hon. friend means by a stampede. They may have been pressure exerted on behalf of Conservatives and also on 'behalf of Liberals. But that is a matter wffiich can be of very little concern to members of Parliament now, or to the public, who naturally -should be interested in the question whether the proposed reform is- in the interests of the country and in the interests of wise, sound, and efficient administration of public affairs. What the public aie interested to know is whether in future there w'iil be a strict adherence to the proposals as set forth in the Order in Council, which we propose shall hereafter have statutory effect by the Bill we are about to introduce.

My hon. friend says that my criticism is not justified in view of the great reform that the sinners are about to effect. I am a doubting Thomas because I have observed the performance not only of the late Government but of the present one. Let me read the pledge given just prior to the election -by the Prime Minister, the leader of the Union Government.

I was saying that the
reason why we have our doubts as to the sincerity of the Government in the operation of the new Act is that the Prime Minister made a very solemn pledge in the following words on the eve of the election:
Civil Service reform with a view to extending the principle of the present Civil Service Act to the Outside Service and ithus to abolish patronage and to make appointment to the Public Service upon the sole standard of merit. The Civil Service Commission has already been directed to make a report to the Prime Minister as to the necessary steps for that purpose. Such arrangements will be subject to the existing regulations, which will give preference to the appointment of returned soldiers who are duly qualified.
And in the Order in Council passed 19th February, 1918, the Prime Minister adds the following:
The Prime Minister observes that immediately after the announcement of this policy directions were given to each department of the Government that patronage lists in every such department should be thereafter abolished.
So that immediately after the pledge was given the Prime Minister states that directions were given to each department to abolish patronage, and in spite of that'' hundreds of new civil servants were appointed to the various boards, commissions, and departments, and in the Outside Service here at Ottawa, Montreal, and even,
I am told, in Winnipeg. Therefore, it is not surprising if we have ou* doubts as to the sincerity of the Government. When those appointments were made very strong protests came from the Civil Service Federation. The following statement was made:
The Executive begs to record its deep regret in the public interest that patronage appointments have been made since Deoember 17th, especially those made 'recently in Montreal and Ottawa.
(Signed), WALTER TODD, President.
And from Winnipeg came, the following telegram, dated February 17, to Sir Robert Borden:
Desire to express keen disappointment regarding recent appointments to Montreal and Vancouver customs and consequent failure of Government to fulfil' promise to eliminate patronage and recognize merit.
Another from Winnipeg:
This association most emphatically protests appointment of Acres, Postmaster, Ottawa, in direct violation of Government pledges to people and service and demands in interests of public morality and Service, that his appointment be rescinded and made for merit only.
I am told that the Prime Minister, and my hon. friend, to whom a copy of these telegrams was sent, did not even answer. What faith can we have in the promise of the Government that patronage will be abolished even after this Act? We can have none. We had similar promises made by the late Administration before the election of 1911, and what happened? My hon. friend knows only too well that twelve thousand Liberals were dismissed and 23,000 Conservatives -were appointed. I am afraid, as a result of the examples we have had since the election, that the Government will find some means to go back to the same old methods in spite of the istern and unbending Liberals who have been introduced to give new life to the old Administration.

My hon. friend (Mr. Leinieux) may rest assured that his fears will not find any justification in the actions of the Government under the proposed Civil Service Bill. If my hon. friend is anxious that the Government should be aided to implement its pledge to abolish patronage, I am sure he will facilitate the passage of this resolution and the Bill to be founded upon it. My hon. friend read from the declaration of policy which my right hon. friend Sit Robert Borden made prior to the election. That was a pledge of policy to be pursued, .and a statement of fact of what had already been done. It was a pledge that it was the intention of the Government to extend the Civil Service Act to the Outside 'Service, and the statement of fact was that the Civil Service Commission had already been instructed to made an investigation looking towards the legislation necessary for that purpose. That is my recollection of the statement as read by my hon. friend.

The Order in Council that I have quoted contains the pledge of the Prime Minister, and he- adds the following words:
"The Prime Minister observes that immediately after the announcement of this policy directions were given to each department ot

the Government that patronage lists in every such department should be thereafter abolished.

The declaration of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister contained a statement of fact Its well as a statement of policy. It contained the statement of fact which my hon. friend has read: .that patronage lists in the departments should be abolished. My hon. friend knows very well that patronage lists are not lists of appointees all over the country. The patronage lists as commonly known in the departments are lists upon which purchases of supplies are made. Appointments to the public service and the patronage lists existing in the departments are altogether different matters. The statement made by the Prime Minister is absolutely true: that he had sent notice to the departments instructing them that the patronage lists should be abolished and that purchases should be made in the public interest irrespective of these lists. That (policy was further implemented by the Government, just as soon as the Government could deal with the matter by transferring the purchasing for all the departments of Government to the war purchasing commission. Therefore, that, feature of the policy of the Government, and the statement of the Prime Minister when he enunciated that policy, have been carried out to the letter.
Coming back to the question of appointments to the Outside Service, the Prime Minister, as my hon. friend has read intimated that the Civil Service Commission would be asked to make a report as to the steps to be taken to bring the Outside Service under the Civil Service Act. So soon as the election was over, and when there was an opportunity to take the matter into consideration, my hon. friend will see from a perusal of the Order in Council that in the absence of the Prime Minister on vacation, I asked my hon. friend the acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) to take the matter up and he immediately started in with the Civil Service Commission to investigate the matter, and to see what provision should be made to give effect to the policy of the Government, My hon. friend will recollect the unfortunate and terrible disaster that happened at Halifax. The conditions following that disaster absorbed a great deal of the time of the acting Minister of Finance. Under these circumstances, it was not possible for him to make the same progress in dealing with the matter as he would have been able to do had he not been obliged to go to Halifax. It so happened,

therefore, that the matter was not ripe for consideration and action when the Prime Minister returned. Upon his return, the Prime Minister took the matter up with the acting Minister of Finance and the Civil Service Commission, and an Order in Council was formulated as soon as the necessary provisions could be worked out between the members of he Government and the Civil Service Commission.
My hon. friend will bear in mind that certain appointments could only be legally made by Order in Council. Under the law as it stood, appointments to the Inside Service were made under the Civil Service Act upon the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission, but no similar provision existed for making appointments to the Outside Service. Until new Orders in Council were passed, until the Civil Service Commission was authorized to deal with appointments to the Outside Service it necessarily followed that the old method of appointment continued. The pledge of the Prime Minister that he would have this matter investigated has been carried out, the Order in Council has been passed, and now the legislation is submitted to the House.
With reference to the number of persons involved in this change, I am sorry that I have not the exact figures here. I did not know that this matter was coming up at this time, but my recollection is that there are in the Inside Service about 5,000 persons and in the Outside Service about 35,000. You cannot make a change affecting such a large number of officials without the necessary careful consideration and preparation by the Civil Service Commission. You cannot at one stroke transfer to a commission which has been dealing with 5,000 employees in the Inside Service the burden of dealing with 35,000 employees throughout the whole Dominion. You must give consideration and serious thought to the details necessary to work out such a radical change. I think it must be conceded by all that this is the most radical proposal in the way of Civil Service reform that has ever been made on this continent at least, and I think I am safe in saying that it is the most radical that has ever been made at one stroke in any country.
Mr. Acres' appointment was not so imperative.

I do not say that any appointment was imperative. Appointments were made under Order in Council because that was the necessary and legal course until a new policy was legally put into effect. Mr. Acres was appointed under the law that was then in force. My hon. friend, the acting Minister of Finance, is correct in saying that

what the country is interested in is the fact that this reform is to go into effect. If all the comment that has been made in reference to two or three appointments, which, it is said, were political appointments, is justified, what is the country going to be saved from when this legislation goes into effect and when 35,000 appointments from one end of Canada to the other will no longer be political appointments as they have been in the past, but will he non-political appointments under the provisions of the Civil Service Act? That indicates the character and extent of the reform.
One word more and I am through. My .hon. friend referred to one appointment of which I have particular knowledge and, therefore, I wish to mention it. He referred to the appointment of Mr. Nichols ais a relative of t'he Minister of Finance and as a Conservative appointment pressed in before the election. iMtr. Nichols was not appointed ibecause, but in spite of the fact that, he was a relative of a member of the .Government, and he was appointed after consultation with gentlemen of the press, because he was represented as the best newspaper man whom we could find who would be available to become director of public information and carry on that work for the Government. He was appointed solely because he was believed to be the best man for the position, and in spite of his relationship. And I can say this further: As (far as the Minister of Finance was concerned he did not know that the appointment was under consideration, or in fact anything about it, until the proposal was submitted to Council. I know that because the appointment came under my personal charge, and it was made on my own recommendation.
If you get your neighbour to make an appointment, it is no better justification than if you put the appointment through yourself.

I have already given
my hon. friend my word that the Minister of Finance knew absolutely nothing about it, and that the appointment was made on my recommendation.

That does not improve
matters at all.
Mr. iROWELL: I do not know what my hon. friend means when he says " if a man gets has neighbour to do it."

I will tell you what it
means. It means that the Minister of Trade and Commerce |may appoint the Prime Minister's brother, to a Government 'position, and in return the Prime Minister may appoint to an office some relative of the Minister df Trade and Commerce. That explanation does not justify the appointment.
Mr. 'E. LAPOINTE: It is the return of a courtesy. Here we have an exemplification of the advantages of Union Government,

The courtesy has not
yet been returned.
It may he expected.

I repeat that the appointment of this gentleman was made after consultation with gentlemen of the press who represented him as- the best newspaper man available for this important and responsible post. It was not made because he was a Conservative, a Liberal would under like circumstances have 'been taken just as quickly. >M^ hon. friend (iMr. Bureau) may feign surprise, but the statement is nevertheless true.

I now have the second
Order in Council, dated February 28, 1918, that was referred to this afternoon. It is as follows:
Whereas doubt has arisen as to whether the Order in Council of the 13th day of February,

1918, (P.C. No. 358) respecting appointments bo, promotions in, and other matters relating to the Civil Service, applies to officers, clerks and employees other than those employed in the several departments, and it toeing desirable to remove any such doubts;

When we rose at six o'clock, the President of the Council was making statements which rather excited my curiosity. He stated-if I am in error, he will correct me, because I do not wish to misrepresent him-that Mr. Nichols' appointment was made in spite of the Minister of Finance "(Sir Thomas White).
I said, not because of, but in spite of, his being a relative.

My error appears to be a grammatical one; I think that I understood my hon. friend rightly. We have known Mr. Nichols as the editor of a Montreal newspaper, and as such he must be fairly known to all other newspaper editors. The member for Russell (Mr. 
Murphy) was talking the other night about the relations between the President of the Council -and certain newspapers. It would seem that my hon. friend himself, therefore, knows something about newspapers.
I did not catch my hon. friend's last remark.
I understood the member for Russell to intimate that the President of the Council was himself connected with newspapers.
No, -that is incorrect.

I am glad to accept the correction. But it was important that my hon. friend communicate with other newspaper men if he desired to obtain a man who had the necessary qualifications as a publicity agent. As a matter of curiosity and of information, may I ask the President of the Council whether he consulted editors of such Toronto newspapers as the Star, Mail and Empire, News, World and Telegram; or of such Montreal newspapers as the Star and the Gazette; or of the Winnipeg Tribune or Winnipeg Free Press? Of course, down home, we do not get the coast newspapers.
The Orange Sentinel.

The proprietor of that paper, being in the House, could be consulted now, if not then. That, however, would depend on the judgment of the President of the Council. No. I want to know what editors or members connected wnn any of those newspapers were consulted.

My hon. friend asks me if any editors or members connected with some of the papers named were consulted. I can say, yes, but I d-o not think that when a minister of the -Crown consults parties with reference to matters relating to appointments in the public service, it is wise to disclose confidences, where there are confidential communications.

I just came in when the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) was speaking. Was the hon. mem-

ber criticising the appointee as being incompetent?

While I agree with the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) that Mr. Nichols is a journalist of . standing, I do not accept the reasoning of the President of the Council when he says that he cannot state under what recommendations Mr. Nichols was preferred to others. I am told by reliable parties, who belong to the press, that many others could have been selected for the post to which Mr. Nichols was appointed. More than that,
I am told that the position itself was not required at all.
That may be.

That is not the
question.

I would like to put a question to the President of the Council. Mr. Nichols is an excellent journalist. He was at one time in Montreal publishing the Daily Mail and the Evening News. I may say. by the way, that he killed both papers. The President of the Council is, perhaps, not familiar with conditions in Montreal.
I know that while he was leader of the Liberal party in Ontario he had to read many newspapers published in his own province. I may tell him that for months and months Mr. Nichols and his two organs in Montreal, the Daily Mail and the Evening News, never ceased to attack most bitterly a gentleman who was in the late Government. I refer to the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes), a dear friend of mine, as hon. members all know. I have heard the ex-Minister of Militia complaining in this House to the Minister of Finance in regard to those attacks. He referred to them in many of his speeches. He said that there was a conspiracy in the Government against him and that Mr. Nichols was the instrument to carry out that conspiracy. Let us come to the point at issue. It is amazing to me that any thoughtful Canadian who has watched the working of the patronage system in this Dominion for the last thirty, forty or fifty years, should not hold up both hands in support of any effort, if this effort is being honestly made, to strike a death blow at the patronage system.

I have stated that I am in favour of the resolution. The effort 
of my hon. friend in picturing - me as trying to destroy the efforts of the Government is unnecessary, and his statement is groundless. I am trying to get some information. When the Civil Service Commission is asked to conduct an examination, or to judge as between A, B. C and D, and award the recommendation to the man who wins the prize, that is the purpose of the Civil Service Commission, but I cannot see how the thing is to work out, or how this commission is going to get information as to petty appointments all over the country. My point, with respect to that class of small appointments is that the Government is not going to make things any better. He might say: "Well, let well enough alone." I do not say, "Let well enough alone," I adfnit the trouble; I know the tremenduous harm that is done by patronage. But patronage may be honestly and fairly administrated, or it may be	abused.	The	idea	that every
appointment that has been made under the patronage system is a bad one, is a delusion. Three out of four men appointed to office have served the country well. I hope it will.

I believe that the hon.

I knew of no less partisan 'bodies than the municipal councils.

Mr. Chairman, I
am very much in favour of this resolution. The Civil Service Commissioner whose salary is named in this resolution should he a man of the very highest integrity. He should be above any government; like the Auditor General, he should be in a position to tell the Government to go to Hades if it does not do what was right.

At the beginning of a new Parliament one gets many surprises. I must say that the greatest surprise I have received yet in this Parliament was in finding any disposition on the part of the member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), or the member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) to hang on to some belief in the old doctrine that " to the victors belong the spoils." The member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) put his finger on the essence of what the Government is trying to obtain in the destruction of patronage. It is, as I conceive it, to separate the member of Parliament from the appointments in his constituency. What would happen if we could accomplish that? In the first place, the people of the country who are civil servants would know that they held their positions upon their merits, and would give their service accordingly. In the second place, the whole of the people would, at election time, vote upon public questions as they conceived those questions would work out for the public good, and not for their own private emolument. That is what would be the effect upon the people; what would be the effect upon members of Parliament? Knowing that the people were going to vote upon the merits of public questions, candidates for Parliament would inform themselves upon public questions and would stand upon their intellectual and political merits for election, not upon their ability to go in for what my friend opposite has called corruption. That is the gist of the whole matter as it appears to me. Can any member of this House who considers the question from that point of view fail to see that if we cayy out this principle it will immensely elevate the public life of the country? That is what I mean by the abolition of patronage in this particular aspect. As to who should make the appointments in small country post offices, in my part of the world it has been a very great difficulty to get men to take office at all. In many cases, when asked for a recommendation, I have simply -written a letter to the department, saying: Ask the inspector to go there -and get the best man he can, whatever his political colour may be. 'The member for Fron'tenac e-ays that he knows the people in his district better than certain other

-men can know them. That is just the trouble with a great many of us; we have known the districts, and known -the men. We all know-let us get rid of cant in this matter-that men have been appointed by members of all political -complexions with the expectation that political services would be rendered -for the appointments. Now, that should go. Men should be appointed to serve the public because of their merits, they should be promoted because of their merits, and they should foe free to act for the public good at election time just as members should be -allowed to stand for the -public good and for the public good only, -and to stand for public questions on their merits. I repeat that if that can be brought about-, it -will immensely elevate the public life of the country and make for the good of Canada.
I want to say this on behalf of the Government:	No sane man expects them to
produce in one moment a perfect scheme for this change, -in all the manifold * complexities of this great country and its public services. But in making an honest endeavour to 'begin to do it, they deserve the sympathy of every right-thinking person in the country. They certainly have my sympathy; they will h-ave all the help that I can give them; and if they go on courageously in the -way they are beginning, they -will have the encouragement of all the best-thinking people in large portions, at any rate, of this Dominion. So far as the next election goes, if anybody is looking so far -ahead, he will stand much better under this system than if be bad hung on to the old method of giving enough jobs to get enough votes to be returned to Parliament.

If I gave my hon.
friend the impression that I proclaimed the doctrine that "to the victor belongs the spoils," or that I was anxious to cling to the system of the distribution of patronage, then I can only say that I failed to -speak iwith that clearness which I always endeavour to attain, though I may not always succeed. I have no desire to do either one. I have never proclaimed the doctrine that " to the victor belongs the spoils," in the sense in which the words are commonly used-though there is a sense in which the words might be legitimately applied. Nor do I desire to cling to patronage. I have had some experience of it, and it lias not been exactly in the line that my Mon. friend suggests. His idea is that when one is instrumental in getting one of his friends a public office, he expects to be re-

warded with political support. Well, that is nut my experience. On the contrary, when I have had opportunity of recommending a man for any public office and the question of political support has come up, I have always told him: My friend, your party services have had something to do with your getting the office, but from this time forward your are the servant of the community, and I do not want you to meddle in politics. That has been my experience in the administration of patronage. The only point of my observations was to call attention to the difficult position in which the Civil Service Commission was being placed. I frankly said in reply to the member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) that I could not at the moment suggest anything better. But I was pointing out that while the Civil Service Commission would be an excellent body to hold examinations, to test qualifications, to decide as between A, B, C, and D for any particular office-that is the duty they were originally intended to discharge, and they -are well qualified to discharge it

yet where there canjbe no examination and no test, nothing more than an inquiry somewhere, the Civil Service Commission were in no better position to get information of that character than anybody else.

I also, Mr. Chairman, want to repudiate the suggestion that I am one wrapped up in the theory, that "to the victors belong the spoils." I am sure that every member of this House would gladly wash his hands of appointments even to a $50 or a $150 job. It is not that we want that work, for political or any other reasons. But I say again that I do not see how it will be possible for the Civil Service Commission, sitting in Ottawa, to ascertain the proper persons to appoint to these positions without applying to those who might be reasonably expected to know who were qualified for them. I repudiate the reflection which I maintain is to a certain extent thrown upon members of Parliament generally by the wording of this resolution and by some of those who are supporting it. In effect, you ,are saying that no man who has been chosen as a representative of the people to sit in this House can be trusted to make an honest recommendation or to select an efficient man to fill a vacancy in the Civil Service. I have had the privilege of sitting as a member of this House since 1908, and I have honestly endeavoured, whenever it has fallen to my lot to recommend a man for a position, to recommend
a man who, I believed, would ,perform the duties of that office efficiently and well, and in doing so I was not thinking about the next election. I believe, when I say that, I am speaking, not for myself alone, but for scores of members in this House. It is not fair to say, because it has fallen to our lot as members of Parliament to recommend men to fill vacancies in the Civil Service, that in our recommendations we were thinking about the votes we were going to get. That is putting members ..of Parliament on a very low plane.

If the Government succeed in placing the Outside Service under the control of the Civil Service Commission, they will have done something to justify their return to power. I wish to endorse very heartily the statements made by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). If Civil Service reform is to be a success in this country, it will not depend so much upon the Government or upon the Civil Service as upon the individual private members representing the various constituencies throughout the Dominion. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) made some reference to the Inside Civil Service in the city of Ottawa. Complaints have been heard with regard to the Inside Civil Service, but I believe the blame rests upon the shoulders of the private members. We all know how every hon. member has in the past used his influence, and notwithstanding what the hon. member for Frontenac says to the contrary, hon. members have in the past used their endeavours to secure for their political friends positions in the Government service, whether at Ottawa or in any other part of the country. The question is: Are we going to be willing to sacrifice what might be termed a political vested right and uphold the work of the Civil Service Commission, or are we going to endeavour to retain in some slight degree control of these appointments throughout the Dominion of Canada? If we undertake to retain control over the minor offices or the major offices, Civil Service reform in this country will be a failure. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (M.r. Fielding) seems to anticipate there will be difficulty in connection with appointments to minor positions. I do not see how there need be any difficulty. As the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) have pointed out, we have inspectors travelling throughout the Dominion in connection with the post office, customs, inland revenue, and those

inspectors are the men who should be responsible to the Civil Service Commission in regard to seeing that appointees to minor positions are fully qualified. When you get down to the lowest class, such as the men who draw $100 or $150 a year, it may be for the position of a janitor or a porter, my contention has always been that the man who has charge of the post office, or the land office, or the customs office, in which a janitor is required, should have vested in him authority to hire a man to carry on that work. If the man who is at the head of that office has not the intelligence and good judgment to hire a janitor or a porter, that man should be removed from his position and a man capable of doing that work and making such appointments named in his stead. After an appointment of that kind has been made, it should be reported to the Civil Service Commission, and the appointee should hold his position unless he is removed from it for good cause.
I just wish again to point out to hon. members that in my opinion the success or the failure of the Civil Service in this country rests almost wholly upon the private members. If they will keep their hands off, if they will not importune the members of the Civil Service Commission to appoint friends to positions, if they will not use their political influence on behalf of those in whom they are interested, I believe the Civil Service Commission will do their work in a manner which will be a credit to that department. Otherwise, Civil Service reform will be a failure.
