I do not believe the Civil Service Commission should, at any time, except in unavoidable cases, bring from some outside district men into, -say, my district, to fill ordinary positions in the Civil Service. There may, at times, be positions which require men having special training, but as regards ordinary positions carrying salaries of $100 a month or thereabouts, in the customs, railways and .so on, il presume every constituency of the 234 constituencies in 'this country can supply men oap-alble of filling such positions. A rule should be laid down that the Civil Service Commission should he instructed in so far

as possible to fill those positions with men selected from the particular constituency in which a vacancy arises.

In filling the positions
will any regard be given to the different political parties? A vacancy might occur in one locality and many people -might Ibe qualified to fill it. It does not require high qualifications to fill the position of postmaster of a small -place. When selections are -being made, how will the officers of the Post Office Department be instructed to make selections?
Mr. A. K. 'MACLEAN:	They will find
out iby some means or another.
<Mr. PBOULX: It will probably depend -much on the political complexion of the officer. 'It he lie in -sympathy with the Government, he will endeavour to find -a person who as known to be a supporter of the Government. If the officer is a supporter of the Opposition, he will probaibly want to -select a Liberal. At the last election we were given pledges by the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues that there iwas to toe no more patronage. The Premier stated there would be -an equal division of the seats in the Cabinet amongst the Conservatives and Liberals. We have not reached that stage yet, tout we expect to reach it. The other day the Premier said that he was going to implement his pledge, and that Liberals and Conservatives would occupy the -same nu-mtoer of seats in the Cabinet. When he made that -pledge, we expected that in appointments to the Senate, regard would Ibe had to the two political parties supporting the Government. Since that pledge iwas given, about a dozen appointments have been made, to the Senate, -and I do not think one Liberal has been appointed. Perhaps the Prime Minister meant by that fifty-fifty basis, that fifty Conservatives would toe first appointed, and then perhaps some Liberals. It might turn out the same way with the Civil Service Commission, that under the guise of no patronage and an equal share to both parties, only members of one party might be appointed. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) said a few minutes ago that there was more efficiency in the Outside Service than in the Inside. There may be a reason for this. The qualifications for the Outside Service are not as high as those for the Inside Service. I am pretty much of the opinion of my hon. friend that in the case of these minor appointments it will be just as hard

for the Civil Service Commission to find properly qualified persons as for members of Parliament, and perhaps harder.
And sometimes easier.
Perhaps.

Frequently the
Civil Service Commission -will fill a vacancy much more quickly than if it were left to a member of Parliament. I have known of vacancies in highly important offices remaining unfilled for perhaps one or two years because the member of Parliament in control of the patronage could not make up his mind what person he would nominate.

So far as that is concerned I agree with my hon. friend. I am in favour of abolishing patronage. I think it would be a good thing for members on both sides of the House. But, as the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) has said, in the practical working out it might be more difficult for the Commission than for members of Parliament to make a selection.
If the Government will carry out this resolution as it is on the Order paper, it will be the greatest step in advance, in my judgment, that has taken place in this country for many years.

I wish to draw the minister's attention to a report of the Committee of the Privy Council, approved on the 18th March, 1918, as follows:
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 16th March, 1918, from the right hon. the Prime Minister, stating that application has been made to the heads of several departments for the dismissal of public officials on the ground1 of offensive partisanship during the recent election.
The Prime Minister observes that the power to dismiss upon such consideration should be sparingly exercised.
It seems to me that that word "sparingly" is utterly opposed to the principle of the Bill. Might I have some explanation from the minister.

As I understand
it, this Order in Council is a direction to the Civil Service Commission that any dismissals made by them should he made only after very careful consideration, and for some offence-against the state for example, *or for dereliction of duty. The last paragraph of the Order in Council reads:
The Prime Minister, therefore, recommends that in no case shall any dismissal for such a cause he made except after reference to the Civil Service Commission ,and with the approval of that Commission, after such inquiry
and investigation as the Commission may deem desirable in the public interest. In reaching a determination the Commission shall have regard solely to the question whether the public interest will be better conserved by the retention or by the dismissal of the official in question and shall take into account his efficiency, the length of his service and the relevant circumstances which may enable them to reach a conclusion.

What are the
relevant circumstances and what about the first part of the Order in Council?

I do not feel I
should detain the Committee in explaining the Order in Council. After all, the portion I have read is the important part, because it contains the declaration of the policy of the Government in respect to dismissals.

I think the first
part is just as important as the last.

The first part
states:	'	.
Application has been made to the heads of several departments for the dismissal of public officials on the ground of offensive partisanship during the recent election.
That means that since the last election very many requests have been made to the, heads of the different departments of the Public Service in Ottawa for the dismissals of persons who at the last election opposed the present Ministry.
Mr. ARiCHAMBAUiLT: The first recommendation of the Prime Minister is important.
Mr. A. K. [MACLEAN: The Prime Minister only made one recommendation, and it was contained in the portion I read, that dismissals be made only after due consideration by the Civil Service Commission.
Read the other part.

The Prime Minister observes that the power to dismiss upon such consideration should be sparingly exercised and he is of the opinion that, having regard to the policy adopted with regard to appointments to the public service, as set forth in the Order in Council approved on the 13th day of February, 1918, dismissals for such a cause should only be authorized in flagrant cases and' subject to the conditions hereinafter set forth.
I submit to my hon. friend who interjected this matter quite irrelevantly into this debate that there is nothing in that to give cause for criticism. The purpose of the Order in Council is quite obvious, I think, to any person who wishes to read and understand it. It means that since

the last election a great number of applications have been made for the dismissal of persons who at the last election opposed this Government. In my hon. friend's own province, I suppose, there was hardly a person holding a Government position who was friendly to this Government at this last election, and there naturally came to the Government requests-

My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) *must not think that any inquiries which have been made on this side meant that we were opposed to the principle of the Bill. In fact, as my hon. friend will remember, the idea of Civil Service reform has been a Liberal idea. If has been advocated on this side of the House for a number of years. The fault that has constantly been found on this side of the House is that the .ight hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) who leads the Government did not implement the promises which he had constantly made before each general election for years past. )It 'was a favourite pastime of the Prime (Minister to promise Civil Service reform. The only actual Civil Service reform that has been carried out in this country was carried out under the leadership of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition ('Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and is contained in the statute of 1908. Wd want this Act to be improved, if any improvement can be made in it, and we are back of the Government in any genuine reform of the Civil Service. My hon-friend, ('Mr. A. K. Maclean) must not try to convey to- the country the impression that the Liberal party is opposed to Civil Service reform because some questions have been asked from this side of the House. On the contrary, we have been preaching it for years and we are advocating it now.
Mr. IMUiRPHY:	With the principle on
which this resolution is supposed to be founded !I am in the most complete sympathy. Any citizen of Ottawa who has spent all his life in this city, and who has had anything at all to do with public life, will very strongly support any measure calculated to remove political patronage. I am not going to weary the committee at this stage of the discussion and at this hour of the night, with any recital of what the members for the city of Ottawa have had to undergo in the past, and possibly have to undergo even yet, in connection with patronage. But I can assure you, that, although I have not the honour to

represent the city of Ottawa, the county which I do represent in this House includes a portion of the city of Ottawa, that portion in which His Excellency the Governor General resides. He is a constituent of mine. - He has never voted for me, but having regard to the resolution under discussion, perhaps it is proper for me to add that neither has he asked me for a job or to appoint anybody to a posi-. tion; so that, I have no complaint about patronage on that score.
The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has said that patronage is a curse. Most heartily do I echo that designation. It is such a curse that my continual wonder has been that men on both sides of politics would put up with it for the length of time that it has endured. I remember that when I was Secretary of State I was 'summoned one day to the office of the Governor General of Canada, the representative of His Majesty the King, to discuss a matter of urgent public business. When the messenger entered my room I was engaged in a wrangle with an individual who insisted that I should appoint him to the position of, what do you think?-ash sifter. Aish sifter! It was useless for me to tell him that there was no such position, useless for me to tell him that I could not create such a position; he demanded it as his right as a free man and a citizen of Canada. I had never heard of or seen him before, and I never want to see him again. That man was the cause of my delaying the Governor General, the representative of His Majesty, fifteen minutes while I discussed that important question of patronage. However, that is an extreme case, but it is an exiperience that is liable to happen to any member of any Government should a hungry office seeker of that type succeed in invading his office. That is only a very minor example of what people have to undergo in Ottawa in connection with patronage.
During the discussion of this resolution a question was asked by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) regarding the provision in the resolution for the payment of a salary of $6,000 to the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Miaclean) was not quite sure whether that wms the same salary as had previously been paid or was an increase of $1,000. If my hon. friend will recall the circumstances connected with the creation of the Civil Service Commission and its personnel, he will remember that the com-

mission as first appointed consisted of two commissioners, Mr. Shortt and Mr. Laro-chelle, each receiving a salary of $5,000. Neither of these gentlemen was appointed chairman, but by reason of dominating the work of the commission, Mr. Shortt succeeded in having the public address him as the chairman, and he never objected to the title. There was no chairman as a matter of fact. Then the personnel of the commission was increased to three, and provision was made that the last appointed would be chairman of the commission. The three present members of the commission are Hon. Dr. Roche, one of our late colleagues in this House; Mr. Clarence Jamieson, another respected colleague of ours in thfe late Parliament, and Mr. Larochelle. Dr. Roche is chairman of' the commission. This is a provision for increasing by $1,000 the salary previously paid and it is for the Chairman.
The hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) in the course of his last remarks, stated that this was the most ininteresting Parliament in the history of Canada. By dint of repeating that they have abolished patronage, the members of this Government, or at least some of them, seem to believe that patronage actually has been abolished. I do not blame them for that but I wish to point out, particularly to my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) who expressed the belief that the Government was honestly trying to eliminate patronage, how difficult it is for those members of the committee, and particularly for any person who has lived in the city of Ottawa and who has knowledge of what is going on, to accept that statement without qualification. With the copy of a letter in my pocket written by one of the members of this Government to a correspondent telling him that he would be placed on the patronage list for orderfe in his line of business, I think I would be doing violence to my common sense if I should accept without qualification the statement that patronage has been abolished.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN; That has no reference to this resolution.

I propose to show that
it has.

What about the Order
in Council?

If my hon. friend will
hear with me I propose ,to show that it has, because this resolution, and the Bill to be founded upon it are designed to "eliminate

political patronage in the control and management of the said Service."
And the patronage list.

My hon. friend from
Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has been good enough to point out that the phrase "patronage list " appears in the Order in Council which hae been brought down, which is supplementary to the resolution under discussion and which is supposed to form part of the basic upon which the new Act will be founded. Now in addition to this letter, which was written by a member of the present Cabinet, after this Union Government was formed, I heard, as I entered the Chamber, discussion as to the appointment of Mr. Nichols.
Was that letter sent after the election?
No. It was a well-timed letter sent just before the election.
After the pledge?

I heard discussion as I entered the Chamber about the appointment of Mr. Nichols to the position of Director of Public Information, and I heard the tribute paid to Mr. Nichols by my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson). As far as I am concerned I do not controvert what the hon. gentleman said with regard to Mr. Nichols in the slightest degree; but the whole point is, and 1 was glad to see my hon. friend from Springfield qualify his observation, whether the position was necessary or not. The position, I unhesitatingly say, was not necessary. Mr. Nichols had made a failure ot a newspaper enterprise in Montreal. He was, in the language of the day, " down and out." He is the half-brother of-I do not know whether he is Minister of Finance -but in any event, the half-brother of Sir Thomas White. He was a good fellow, no doubt. He was a supporter of the Government and a job had to be provided for him. The position of Director of Public Information was created at a salary of $5,000 a year to impress the public of Canada how entirely and sincerely devoted this administration is to the winning of the war. Now with that fact within our knowledge, I submit to my hon. friend from Springfield it would be doing violence to our common sense to accept unqualifiedly the declaration of the Government that they have eliminated political patronage.
In the city of Ottawa there is a publication known as the Civilian, a very'ably and well written paper, which is the official organ of the civil servants under the present Government. In issue after issue since the date of the election that paper has specifically charged this Administration with the exercise of most reprehensible forms of patronage. That paper in one or two issues made, in point of fact, a most shocking charge against the Administration in con-dectibn with appointments to some of the departments, a charge to which this evening I shall do no more than allude, but to which it may be necessary for me to return later on. I have not heard, and I do not believe, that these charges were challenged by the Government; in any event if they were so challenged I have not heard that any punishment has been meted out to the person responsible for making these charges over his own signature; and certainly if the charges could not be sustained, then the man or men who made them would merit, not only public dismissal but public punishment. I have not heard that anything of that kind has been done, and so while the record in that regard remains as it is, again I say it would be doing violence to one's common sense to accept without qualification a statement that patronage has been abolished.
By word of mouth.

Just about the time that this Order in Council was passed to which my hon. friend the acting Minister of Finance referred this afternoon and this evening and from which he has read extracts, we had, synchronizing, as his predecessor (Sir Thomas White) would say, with its passage, one of the most flagrant exhibitions of political patronage that ever occurred in the city of Ottawa, or in the public service of this country, and that is saying a good deal. We had an exhibition of political patronage which has spread disaffection through the whole body of civil servants, not only in Ottawa, but elsewhere throughout the Dominion. Civil servants, by reason of this happening, have reached the conclusion that unless through the accident of family relationship, or by reason of coming within the favoured class so delicately alluded to in the letter which was read by the hon. member from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Read) they have very little hope of receiving justice at the hands of this Administration. Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens' (Mr. Fielding) and I think my hon. friend the acting Minister of Finance also, will be aware that the former Auditor Genera], as well as the present Auditor General, and the members of the Treasury Board under

the last two Administrations, took no position more strongly against innovations, or violations of the Civil Service Act and the Superannuation Act, than they did in connection with attempts to add more years of service to the term of service of the civil servant who wanted to retire. And yet, Sir, this Government claims it has abolished patronage, and the members of it comport themselves in public as if they actually believe that statement. These are the hon. gentlemen who are responsible for a transaction referred to in the columns of The Ottawa Citizen of February 14, 1918, and which I propose to read to this
10 p.m. committee. The article in question is an editorial, under the title of, "Sir Robert Borden's Prestige." The text of that editorial is as follows:
The superannuation of Mr. J. W. Borden, paymaster of the Militia Department, may have -been arranged without the Prime Minister being consulted about it. According to the terms of the superannuation and retirement act, in ordinary circumstances, Paymaster-general Borden would seem to have been entitled to a retiring annuity of about $1,600. By a dubious interpretation of certain provisions in the act, the retiring paymaster is being credited1 with five more years service than he has actually given to the state; and in this way it has been arranged for him to draw an annuity of about $2,0'00 ; practically $400 a year more than the ordinary civil service retirement allowance.
Mr. J. W. Borden is being credited with five years more than he has actually served, apparently on the pretext that the office of paymaster-general and accountant is being abolished. When, for reasons of economy and efficiency, certain offices are abolished in the civil service, the retiring official may be credited with extra years of service. But the abolition of the paymaster-general and accountant's office would seem to be something of a legal fiction, hardly in accordance with the spirit of the act. The office by a technicality may be said to have been abolished. Actually it has been divided into two offices paymaster-general's office and accountant's office.
With regard to efficiency and economy, whatever may be said for efficiency, the change could hardly have been made on the basis of war economy. In the place of one paymaster-general and accountant, Mr. J. W. Borden, at $4,000 a year, there has now been installed a paymaster-general, Col. J. G. Langton, at $ 6,000 a year, and one of the present officials of the department-a well qualified one, by the way-has been moved up to the position of accountant at $3,5 0'0 a year. So that, where the position formerly cost the state $4,000 a year, it will now cost, with the superannuation allowance to the retiring paymaster, $11,5-00.
There need be no great objection to the higher salaries. It has been one of the weakness of the Canadian civil service that the permanent officials who do the actual work have been much underpaid. It would perhaps have been more encouraging to the Canadian men overseas, if the position of paymaster had been given to an officer who had actually seen active service. It doefe not enhance the prestige of

the Prime Minister, however, to permit such a dubious interpretation of the superannuation and retirement act as the awarding of an extra allowance to the retirement annuity of Mr. J. W. Borden.
When -Sir George Murray reported to the Prime Minister in 1912, he said of this very practice:
"The provisions of section 12 of the Superannuation and Retirement Act, which enables an addition of years to be made to the actual service of certain persons, are in my opinion of doubtful expediency; and I should prefer to see them withdrawn."
As an instance of precept without example, in public service reform, the employment of this doubtful expediency for the financial benefit of Sir Robert Borden's own brother could hardly have been arranged in any spirit of friendship to the Prime Minister. It must be calculated to have exactly the reverse of a helpful influence with regard to the Prime Minister's resolution to establish Civil Service reform.
Sir George Murray says further of this mode of retirement as employed for IMr. J. W. Borden's benefit:
"Under the act the grant of the additional years is personal to the individual and depends on the view which may be taken, either at the time of his appointment or at the time of his retirement, of his qualifications, and on other considerations of a less relevant character. This involves a good deal of rather invidious discussion, which would be avoided if the grant depended not upon the individual but on the qualifications required for the office which he happened to hold."
When certain other cabinet ministers are desirous of perpetuating the business of political patronage, and debasing the Civil Service into a political machine, in spite of all the Government's pledges, they could not employ more subtle ways than by involving Sir Robert Borden personally in an evasion of the spirit of Civil Service reform, and in the countenancing of patronage influence in Civil Service changes.

Our friends on the other side seem to have a desire to reproach gentlemen on this side with opposition to the resolution. We are all in favour of this resolution; all we want is to get information. We see by the Order in Council which I had the pleasure of procuring since six o'clock, that the Government has gone to a good deal of trouble. There have been conferences will the Civil Service Commissioners, conferences with-the law officers of the various departments, and with the Parliamentary Counsel. The acting Minister of Finance seems to think that because this resolution is introduced by the Union Government, we must swallow it and say nothing; that we must regard it as the great benediction of the year. As the acting minister has said, if the purposes which appear to be aimed at by this proposed measure, accomplish the results which we
hope for, it will certainly be a good thing for the country.
Then why not let the resolution go through?

We want it to go through, and that is why we want to throw some light upon it; so that my friend will be able to draft a Bill that will meet the desire of all members of the House, and so that he will go down to posterity as the choker of the great evil and -curse of this country, patronage.
I prefer to have all the light my hon. friend can give me when he has the Bill before him and is in a position to know exactly what he is- talking about.

And I prefer that my
hon. friend bring down a Bill carefully prepared-he has the machinery to do it; he has the men with whom he can take counsel; he 'has the Civil Service Commission-and be in a position to give reasons for every clause in it.

The Bill is
ready, and if my hon. friend is desirous of getting light, why does he not allow the resolution to go through-or, at least, discuss the resolution, itself?

Instead of losing his
tamper; instead of singing with his mellow voice " Carried " when we get up to speak, why does my hon. friend not take notice of what we say, so that, in conjunction with hie advisers, he may be able to bring down a Bill which will ,be satisfactory to the House and based upon such conclusions and such information as may be derived from this discussion? It is true that the Bill, if founded only on what is contained in the Order tin Council or the resolution, will ibe imperfect; but what I got up particularly to say was that my hon. friend ought not to accuse gentlemen on this side of the House with opposing the resolution. We are in favour of the resolution, but we have a right to ask for information. Last night we passed a Bill, and we were told: wait until next Parliament; we will then provide the machinery. We do not want to support a Bill which is simply an -enunciation of policy; we want to establish the machinery that will give effect to this proposed measure. My hon. friend, therefore, should go a little more into detail; if he has further information to give to the House, and wait until he brings down the Bill, it may then be too late. He will say:



why not let this Bill go through; we want to make an experiment; next year we will see where the defects are and at the next session we will bring down a new Bill.
A moment ago my hon. Mend said he was going to make an inquiry in regard to the Bill, and he has not made the inquiry. If he has not made the inquiry, I am wondering why he rose.

That would not be the
first time that my hon. friend would be wondering, not only at my rising, but at other things.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No one wonders when the hon. member rises.

I am glad that somebody can realize" why I rise. I was going to ask if this resolution was introduced for the purpose of discussion, or if it was only introduced for the purpose of throwing it down upon the Table with the statement by [DOT]the Minister of Finance:	I have brought
down this resolution; wait until I introduce the Bill; when the Bill is introduced, swallow it? This resolution is brought down for the purpose of discussion, so that when the Bill comes before the House we shall have a Bill containing suggestions that deserve to be taken into consideration by hon. mem. beTS>. Therefore, if the minister is getting impatient, I may tell him that he need not [DOT]try to convey to this House or the country the impression that we are against the Civil Service Commissions providing patronage' is abolished and providing they will be a check upon the various ministers and will prevent them from writing letters such as the one which has been read here tonight by my hon. friend from Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Read), stating mat everybody who is a Liberal Unionist or a Conservative Unionist may live happily because patronage hereafter will go fifty-fifty.

The hon. senior member
for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) declared ia moment ago that his Bill is ready. I am very sorry it is, because I would suggest that in this Bill should be included a measure of justice to repair the great injury committed by the late Government. During the period of six years from 1911 to 1917, when this new Union Government was formed, the evil of patronage existed; not only did it exist, but, I might say, it bloomed, and not only did it bloom, but it flourished. In the city of Quebec, in which I reside, and in the district of Quebec, a constituency in which I represent, public

officials were thrown out of office. People who had worked for the Government of the country for years, people who had given satisfaction during long periods of years, were thrown out of their positions. Why? Because they had either the fortune or the misfortune to be Liberal when a Tory government was in power. In the city of Quebec, we saw the very sad spectacle of politicians who had become members of Parliament writing letters to the different members of the 'Cabinet at Ottawa recommending that so-and-so should be thrown out because so-and-so happened to be a Liberal and the government was a Tory government. What happened then did not surprise us in Quebec, because we knew the methods of a really Tory government. But now I understand we no longer have a Tory government; that this Government has been improved to such an extent that it is transformed, that from a Tory government it has become a Union Government. I cannot judge of the actions of the Government in the other provinces as I have not *been there, but how has this new, wonderful, Union Government acted towards my province of Quebec? In the same old way as the Tory government which preceded it. I wish to recall to your memory, 'Sir, the very impaitial way in which officials were appointed in the province of Quebec to hold the recent election. Was patronage abolished? The Prime Minister of Canada (Sir Robert Borden) at that time was touring the province of Ontario with the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), if I remember aright, and sometimes with the Solicitor-General. The promise made by the Premier in all the cities in which he spoke was: I have, since the formation of this Union Government, abolished patronage, and this Government, if elected, will introduce legislation to do away with patronage permanently. At the time the Prime Minister was uttering those words, patronage was being exercised by his own colleagues in the province of Quebec in the appointment of electoral officers. Of the enumerators appointed throughout the province of Quebec, not one, in any constituency of which I know, was a Liberal.
Perhaps it was impossible to get any to act.
The result of the election shows that.
1 do not catch exactly what my hon. friend the minister means.
I say that probably it was impossible to get Liberals to act

I am quite sure that if
the returning officer in my constituency had wanted a list of my friends who would ;be willing to act as enumerators, judging *by the majority I secured it would have been easier for me to supply a list than for my opponent to do so, and the same thing is true in every other constituency in Quebec. Not only were enumerators chosen from amongst the Tories, but after the election was over, after the Government was elected with a huge majority, was the system changed in our province? In the city of Quebec, has patronage been abolished? Since coming to the city of Ottawa to represent my constituency in this House, I have seen Tory supporters of the Government in the streets of Ottawa seeking jobs either for themselves or their friends. Would they be here if patronage was abolished?
I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the committee, but we on this side of the House, as the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) has said, are in favour of abolishing patronage, but we want the Government to be in good faith. We do not want the Acting Minister of Finance to say to us: You have to support this measure because I have introduced it.
Mr. A. K. 'MACLEAN: I did not say that.

If the minister did not
say that, he came very close to saying it. Such a statement is no recommendation. We on this side of the House want more than that. The Government, from my experience, apparently has two means of defending measures; either they say:	You
must not talk against this measure because it is a measure to win the war, or they say:	You must not speak against
this measure because we former Liberals introduced it. This is no way of discussing legislation on its merits. If the Government's Bill is good, we shall support it; if it is bad, we shall vote against it. The Government, so that we may be sure that this is a good -measure, has first of all to prove its sincerity. Has the Government proved its sincerity?

speechtext:

Resolution reported and concurred in.
Hon. A. K. MACLEAN thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 53, respecting the Civil Service of Canada.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) Bill No. 3, to confer the electoral franchise upon'women, was read the third time and passed.

On motion of Hon. C. C. Ballantyne (Minister of Naval Service) Bill No. 49, respecting the Naval Discipline (Dominion Naval Forces) Act, 1911, was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Naval Discipline (Dominion Naval Forces) Act, 1911, made applicable to Canada:

Very few of us have had occasion to refer to the Naval Discipline Act enacted by the Parliament of the United

Kingdom. We do not want the details, but perhaps the minister might explain briefly what the effect of this Bill will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In brief, it is this: Suppose the Rainbow is on the Pacific coast, and one of its oflicers has committed a serious breach of discipline, necessitating his trial by court-martial. On that particular boat there may not be an officer of sufficiently high rank to conduct the court-martial. If this Bill meets with the approval of the committee and the House that officer could be tried by a senior officer on board any British, Australian or New Zealand man-of-war that happened to be in the harbour. The Canadian Naval Service would simply call upon that senior officer to preside at the court-martial. It is simply for discipline purposes. I might state that in 1911 the Imperial authorities passed what was known at that time as the Naval Discipline (Dominion Naval Forces) Act, 1911. It did not apply to any of the overseas dominions, unless the parliaments of those dominions saw fit to pass similar legislation to that passed by the Imperial authorities. Australia passed the legislation which we are now asking to have adopted on 12th August,
1913.	New Zealand passed it on 16th July,
1914.	And, inasmuch as the Canadian navy is still very small but at the same time considerably larger than it was some years ago, we thought it necessary, for discipline purposes, that we should be able to have an interchange of officers between any of the ships belonging to England, Australia, New Zealand or any of the overseas dominions.
Mr. McMAS'TER:	Will the minister infore me whether that applies in times of peace, or only in time of war, when the ships of Canada have been placed under the jurisdiction of or are co-soperating with those of Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If this Bill passes the House it will be on the statute books, and will have effect in time of peace ju6t the same as in time of war.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne for the third reading of the Bill:

I understand some hon. gentlemen have further comments about the Bill being in force in times of peace, and in regard to allowing Australian officers to preside at an inquiry on a Canadian ship.
[iMr. Bureau. ]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is a good
opportunity to make those remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
'Canadian officers
have the same privileges as the officers of Australia. Suppose an Australian ship were in Halifax, and one of the junior officers committed a breach of discipline, and it was necessary he should be tried by court-martial, and a Canadian man-of-war had a senior officer on board, the Australian ship could send over to the Canadian ship and get that officer. It is simply for the purpose of holding court-martial-nothing more nor less. Australia has passed similar legislation, as also has New Zealand, and the only country which has not done so is Canada.

I can quite understand and quite approve of the provision that in time of war the navies of the different overseas dominions and of Great Britain should act as one, and that there should be this perfectly free interchange of authority between officers of the different overseas dominions, and of the Motherland, but without very careful consideration, and without strong reasons for the proposal, I am very doubtful whether the proposal tends to what we are all desirous of having, namely, the closest possible spiritual unity between the different British Commonwealths. Frankly, I do not like the idea that in time of peace a servant of the Canadian Government should be tried by court-martial presided over by an Australian. Although the hon. minister informs us Australia passed this legislation, at the same time I do not think it would tend towards unity to have an Australian tried by court-martial presided over by a Canadian. I believe the greatest unity will be brought about if, as far as possible, in times of peace we should all act as one. I desire to insist upon that. And it would be better to have Canadians, if they have made any errors or have infringed the military or naval law in any way, tried by their own fellow-countrymen, and by them alone. Suppose that in one of these trials a miscarriage of justice occurs-and it is possible-what bitter feeling might be engendered. If, say, a Canadian superior officer by some mistake condemned an Australian improperly, I think a very considerable amount of feeling might grow up between Australia and Canada. I would not like this Bill to pass without this aspect of the situation being presented, because I believe those who have thought about the relation which should exist between the different British Commonwealths have come to this

conclusion, that the tie which binds us will be strengthened in proportion as each individual Commonwealth is allowed to work out in its own way what seems best to the citizens of that Commonwealth, and I am afraid that the Bill presented to-night endangers that spirit of unity which I spoke about. I cannot aliow the measure to pass without drawing to the attention of the Government the objection which I have in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: The hon. gentleman moved the adjournment of the debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Under the circumstances, the Bill only having been presented yesterday, I consent to the debate being adjourned. I may say, however, to the hon. gentleman who raised this question (Mr. Bureau), that the Bill only carries out the purpose, as I understand it, which was embodied in the legislation of this House as far hack as 1910. There need not be the slightest anticipation of any difficulty or lack of harmony in working it out. It is merely a Bill designed to assist co-operation between the permanent naval forces in each portion of the Empire, whether in time of peace or war. As a matter of fact, its operation would be practically altogether confined to the time of war; it is extremely improbable that it should ever be invoked in time of peace. It might, but it is a remote possibility, that it will have any effect in time of peace. Its operation, in so far as it would come into operation at all, would be in time of war.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
On Ithe motion of Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals), Bill No. 42, to amend the Department of Railways and Canals Act, was read the second
time, and the House went into Committee on the Bill;, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The minister said the other night that the Government would take the initiative in acquiring the rolling stock and materials that were necessary for the Government and other railways. I understood the minister to say that some of the material so acquired would be apportioned to the Canadian Pacific railway. Am I right in that surmise?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: One hundred thousand tons of rails will go to the Canadian Pacific. The Government will purchase the rails and distribute them amongst the different railways. The Canadian Pacific will get probably half of these rails. It is merely a book-keeping account so far as they are concerned. The rails will be shipped to them and they will immediately pay the -money back to us; or they will pay the Dominion Iron and Steel company for the hundred thousand tons of rails that they get.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I understood the minister to say the other night that he had given orders to the various steel mills for steel for cars and rails?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Also that contracts for freight cars have been given, and that the companies that have received these contracts will get steel through the department for the building of steel frame cars?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
If there is anything
that the Government can purchase for any of these companies cheaper than the companies can purchase it themselves, it will he glad to do so. The Government is able to purchase some things in the United States that a private company probably cannot purchase. In that case the Government will purchase the material and, hand it direct to the car company at whatever is paid for it, in order to be sure that the care will be completed at the earliest possible moment. Last year two or three companies had great difficulty in getting materials on the other side of the international boundary, but as the cars which they had contracted for were to be supplied to the Canadian Government for war purposes we were able, through our representative, to persuade the Washington Government to allow us to have the necessary materials, and we got them probably a little cheaper than the contractors would be able to get them. If we purchased anything of that kind it would simply be to hand it over to the company at the price we paid for it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The question was asked
the minister the other night if the car factories in Canada were in a position to deliver the cars as they were required by the Government. My hon. friend promised that he would bring down a statement or give us an idea of the different kinds of cars that were required and how soon they would be distributed and put in use on the Government railways. Are there in Canada sufficient car factories actually in operation to fill these orders and meet the demands of the Government? We have in Canada shipyards constructing wooden ships. I understand it is the policy of the Government to abandon that completely. I am told by the owners of shipyards now engaged in building wooden ships, that they are well equipped to build wooden ships, as well as steel freight cars. These ships will be launched in June or July and after they are launched the yards will be idle, although they have a complete equipment for building freight cars. Of course, I make that statement on the information of a gentleman who, as the minister knows, is perfectly well qualified to speak upon the subject. One of them has been the managing director of a big car factory in the United States and even in Canada. They say that within a very short time, perhaps within a month, they will be in a position to turn out freight cars at the rate of ten, twelve, and fifteen a day. Rather than see orders go outside of this country to the United States, and allowing these yards and this capital to remain idle, I suggest that in the national interest, it might be well to convert them into car factories. I may tell my hon. friend, surprising as the fact may be, that the men who are employed in the building of these wooden ships are all old men, and it is remarkable to see how actively and skilfully they do the caulking and the other different kinds of work required in shipbuilding. It seems that the wooden ship building is being revived, and it is giving a new lease of life to these old men whose business it had been in days gone *by to build wooden ships. Now, as I say, I raise the question because at the' time I asked my hon. friend this appropriation [DOT]was not before the House, and with the money that he had at his disposal, all the orders that he foresaw to be given, I understood from him, had been given. Now, if I am not mistaken, all these cars have not been ordered, and I would submit that what .1 have suggested be taken into consideration when he distributes the orders for these cars.
TMr. J. D. Reid.l
Mr. ,T. D. REID: The hon. gentleman, as I understand, has asked me if the number of car factories in Canada is sufficient to fill these orders. My information is that tnere are sufficient car factories now equipped in Canada, and have been in operation for some time, to manufacture probably five or six times more than the order that we have been giving and dividing up. If I remember well, the Canada Car Company, with their several plants, [DOT]could manufacture about thirty thousand [DOT]box cars per annum. The Eastern Car Company and the National Car Company of Hamilton can both manufacture several thousand. There are several other factories operating; in fact, the order that we distributed would suffice only to keep one of the factories going but a short time. :If I understand correctly, the Canada [DOT]Car Company, to whom we have given an order for five thousand cars, distributed among the three plants at Fort William. Montreal and Amherst, have taken an order from the American Government for ten thousand cars at a higher price than we are paying. I am informed the contract has been completed, if not, I know that the negotiations have been going on; and the company were very glad to get the order to keep their factory going. The difficulty with these factories is this: Take the Fort William factory. They tell me that it is one of the best equipped car factories in Canada, and even on the continent, with a very large capacity. It was built at the time of the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific and other roads, and then remained idle for some time, but they were enabled with the order for two or three thousand cars which we gave them last year to start the works up again. They have also been engaged in turning out Russian orders as well. However, if they were not able to get any other orders for cars than those that we have given them, I do not think their factory would operate longer than two or three months at the most. Our orders were distributed among those factories that are well equipped) and in operation, and I understand we are to have those cars by the first of September or the first of October for the transportation of wheat and other products.
I may say to the hon. member that the shortage of cars in Canada is causing us a great deal of trouble and creating uneasiness. The hon. gentleman comes from the province of Quebec. Let me tell him that I am very much worried for the reason that

I could ship fifty thousand cars
11 p.m. of pulpwood out of the province of Quebec that are now there awaiting shipment to the United' States, hut I have not got the cars to enable me to do so. The general manager tells me that if we send a box car over there we will not get it back. Ontario is also suffering for the want of cars; the people who are getting out pulpwood and lumber, and so on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: And for the want of the money?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, suffering for the -want of the money also. If we could get the cars to ship these materials over it would help us out very much:	I think 1
have fully answered the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why is it necessary for the Government to purchase this large number of rails for a corporation like the Canadian Pacific? I can understand it being done in the case of the smaller corporations, but why should it be necessary for a corporation of the financial standing of the Canadian Pacific?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The reason is this: The Dominion Iron and Steel company and the .Algoma Steel company are the only two concerns that manufacture steel Tails in Canada. Both of them had orders from the Imperial Munitions Board, and it was necessary to arrange with that board to get them to release one of the companies for a time until we could get some steel rails rolled, in order to enable the main lines to be put into proper condition. Therefore, the Government, under the terms of an Order in Council, required the Dominion - Iron & Steel company to manufacture one hundred thousand tons of rails, which they purchased and immediately divided among the different railways. The rails are invoiced to the Government, the Government sends the invoice to the Canadian Pacific railway and the company promptly pay for them.
Mr. WiIGMORE: Then there is no expense incurred by the Government?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No expense whatever. When the invoice comes to the Department of Railways and Canals we send the account to the Canadian Pacific, and they forward a cheque. That cheque is deposited to the credit of the Receiver General. It is just a matter of book-keeping, and is done in order that we may promptly get and distribute the rails.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Would that also apply to the Grand Trunk?
'Mr. J. D. REID: To the Grand Trunk as well. As for the Canadian Northern, they are financed by the Government, but the procedure is the same.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: During the past two years the Government have taken up a lot of rails, some of them new, and shipped them to the Allies overseas. Are these rails sold to the Allies at about the same price as the Government are paying under this large contract?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I must frankly state that I have not gone into that matter carefully, but I could get the information and give it to the hon. gentleman. As I understand, the rails were taken up mostly in the West, and the cost of taking them up and shipping them is to be added to the cost and paid by the Allies. The rails were mostly taken from the Grand Trunk Pacific, and it was only a short time ago that I was speaking with the president of the Grand Trunk railway about the matter. I am satisfied that the price was adjusted satisfactorily; the amount is charged to the Allies, and there will be no difficulty about that. Of course, they are paying the same for the rails from the Transcontinental as they are for those from the Grand Trunk Pacific.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
These rails were taken up
and sent overseas, and possibly charged to the Allies on the basis of what they cost, plus transportation. The cost of these rails was considerably less per mile than the cost of the rails the minister is now contracting for; consequently, if the rails he is now buying are to be used to replace those sent overseas, so much more will be added to the capitalization of the railway and the Canadian people will have to pay for it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: These rails are not to replace those taken up and sent overseas. Any replacement of this kind will likely not be done until some future time. The only rails taken from the Transcontinental and sent overseas were those in sidings and yards, and they were replaced with secondhand or lighter rails.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Were rails taken up
from the Hudson Bay line?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We have not yet decided to take them up, but if we do so, they will be replaced with lighter rails.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The minister says he has distributed orders for cars. On what basis are the orders given? Are tenders called, or is there a set price for which the companies are to build a special kind of car?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We asked all the car companies to submit tenders and we awarded the contracts accordingly. We asked the several car companies to say how many care they could supply. The Eastern Car Company, Nova Scotia, had an order for 1,080 cars last fall. Although they had a great deal of material on hand, they were unable to get all the material required to complete the order. However, they stated how many they were able to take and we gave them an order for what they could manufacture up to next fall.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: At what price?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: At the lowest price in every case. We did the same with the Hamilton Car company, which had an order for 1,000 cars about a year ago. They completed the order about the 1st of May, and then wanted a further order for 1,000 cars.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Was the price the same.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The tender of the Hamilton company was somewhat higher than the others, but they came down to the price of the lowest tender, and we gave them another order for 1,000 cars to keep their plant going. All orders were given within Canada except a total of 50 oil and water tank cars which are not manufactured in this country. These were purchased in Pittsburg at a very low price.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the approximate cost of a 60,000 pound box car?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: About $2,750 complete.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is it the intention of the Government to use the Transcontinental workshops in the city of Quebec?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It would require a good deal of money to put them in working condition. Of course, the whole railway situation will have to be looked into in the near future, and that is one of the matters that will receive attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What steps are being taken to trace the 25,000 cars mentioned by the minister as having been sent to the United States and lost track of? How many box cars have been ordered from the different firms? If 25,000 Canadian cars are in the United States, it would be good business to make a special effort to trace them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I think the number of cars to which my hon. friend refers has been reduced to 11,000 or 12,000. We cannot compel the return of these cars, but I have personally lby telegram and by letter to the

Director General of Railways in the United States made every possible effort to secure their return. The Canadian Railway Defence Asisociation in Montreal have also been doing all they can in this direction. Up to the last month, however, all these concerted efforts have not reduced very much the number of cars which are still outstanding. I have also taken the matter up with Mr. Lloyd Harris, of the war mission, at Washington, and he has been doing all he can to .shave these cars returned.
That shows that every effort has been made. In addition to that, almost every other day I am telegraphing to find out if I cannot have the cars returned to this country. Only this evening, I sent a message to t'he several railway companies in the United States urging them to try and let us have cars to take out the pulpwood and lumber in Quebec and other places. Everything that can be done, either by the railways or by the Government, to get the number of Canadian cars in the United States reduced, is being done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I hope the minister will
not make the mistake that seems to have been made in the United States, of going so far as to place an embargo against Canadian cars going into the United States. The House and the country must remember that our cars do not go into the United States empty, they go there with Canadian goods for which money comes back to us. It would not hurt this country if we had a little reciprocal treatment from the United States and had cars coming into this country loaded .with corn which we need so much. It is largely owing to the War Board in the United States that the railway situation has been tied up. I hope we are not drifting along into the same condition in this country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Last fall, we allowed
cars to enter the United States so as to let our products move out, with the result that the cars that went across the border never returned to Canada. The number of Canadian cars in the United States mounted up to 25,000, and if we had not prevented our cars from crossing the border, the result would have been that we would not have been able to move our own Canadian products from one part of the Dominion to the other. If, at the present time, we were to load our cars with lumber, pulp-wood and other products and rush them into the United States, we would not have cars for our own traffic. Instead of a surplus of Canadian cars being in the United

States, there should Ibe a surplus of American cars in Canada. But when our cars get into the United States, the American railway companies /will ndt return them.
Mr. 'MANION: The car situation is a very important matter. Can the minister impose any penalty upon cars going into the United States? If a car of goods comes here, and it is detained for twenty-four hours in the yards, we have to pay demurrage charges. Why should we not impose some charge on cars going into the United States? If we are allowing our cars to go into the United States and they are being held in the United States, and we have to buy new cars to replace them, I do not see any advantage in that.
iMr. J. D. RBID: We cannot do other than allow the arrangement entered into between the railways and the Interstate Commission to be carried out. A foreign car on any railway is charged a certain per diem rate, and the railway that has that foreign car must pay that rate. At the present time, it pays the United States railway companies to pay that rate and to hold the cars. Let me draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the reason why the United States railway detain our cars. In the United States they have given an order for 100,000 cars and 3,000 engines, which shows the shortage of cars there. Therefore, any railway that can secure any foreign ears and can keep them by paying the per diem allowance, will do so, because it pays them to do so, owing to the great shortage 'of cars. The United States railways are very short of cars, and there is nothing more we can do than we have been doing to get those cars returned. The Government realize that the fact of our businessmen not being able to ship goods to the United States is affecting our trade balance. The necessity of maintaining our trade balance is one thing that makes it imperative for us to do everything possible to have our cars returned to Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is any duty imposed?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There is just a per diem rate. The moment a United States car arrives in Canada, a per diem rate is charged until the car returns to the United States. If a Canadian car goes to the United States, for instance, on to the New York Central, while it is on that road they pay sixty cents a day. That railway can keep that car, because there is no way of compelling it to return it. They might keep it for a year ,by paying, say, $180 for the use of that car.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Hbw is that rate fixed?
.Mr. J. D. REID: By an agreement between our railways and the United States railways.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: A penalty might be imposed by increasing the rate. If it pays the United States' railways to keep our cars over there, we should increase the rate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
In order that that might be accomplished, all the railways would have to agree to it. The Canadian railways could not do it alone, and as the United States railways are so much in the majority, it might 'be a little difficult to make such an arrangement. The suggestion, however, is a good one. Since last fall the Government railways represented by myself, together with some of the other railways, have been doing all we could to get our cars back from the United States; we have reduced the number from twenty-five thousand to ten or eleven thousand, and we hope in the next few months to reduce it still further. That reduction, together with the new cars we are getting, we hope, will put us>
in a much better position than we have been in for some time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The shortage of cars is a very serious problem, and, to a certain extent, the Minister of Railways deserves credit for this legislation, but I am amazed to learn that the same oldi penalty of sixty cents per day represents the demurrage when a car has 'been sent into the United States and has not been returned. The two Governments, having succeeded in establishing a commission on international waterways, a commission which has been working most successfully since its establishment, should establish a joint railway commission. Some years ago, when I w-as in the Government the then chairman of the commission in 'Canada, Mr. Justice Mabee, was authorized, not officially, to enter into negotiations with the commission in the United States. I do not know the result. Mr. Mabee died shortly afterwards, and I do not know if the matter was pursued further. At a time like this, it is of the utmost importance for both countries, having regard to the precedent of the joint commission on international waterways, to find1 a way out of this difficulty by some arrangement between the two railway boards. Since the beginning of the war the Government has been able to reach some conclusions which, before the war, were considered absolutely impossible of solution. Many arrangements that have

been made between the Ottawa Government and' the Washington Government since the war commenced, are to-day considered as matters of course. This is a practical question which will affect relations between both countries for all time to come. My hon. friend, if he is a progressive minister, should see to it that we have a joint arrangement between the Interstate Railway Commission and the Railway Commission in Canada. Last winter, a company with which I am connected had most serious difficulty in securing cars because our cars were in the United States. I appealed to my hon. friend and to the Chairman of the Railway Board and got as much satisfaction as they could1 give me, for which I am thankful. We simply had to Ibeg for these cars and we got them back in driblets. It seems to me that the time has come for my hon. friend to strike a bold blow and make an arrangement with the United Statets for raising the penalty. With a penalty of only 60 cents a day, the companies in the United States will keep cars for months, and probably for years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Chairman of the
Board of Railway Commissioners has been working unofficially with the Interstate Commission and has been doing everything he can to get the cars back. The organization that was established in Montreal by the railway companies has also accomplished something. Their secretary has been travelling backwards and forwards and has been working in conjunction with the American organization. The War Board in New York has also been, working along the line suggested by my hon. friend. It had never occurred to ine before that raising the penalty might have some effect in getting the cars back, but I am to have a meeting with Sir George Bury, Mr. Gillen and other gentlemen connected with this organization next week, and as we had intended to discuss this matter I will bring my hon. friend's suggestion before them. We are anxious to devise some means for getting our cars back and keeping the spread to a minimum, and I am glad to have my hon. friend's suggestion.
