On motion of Hon. F. B. Carvell, the House went into committee on Bill No. 41, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Definition of work:
Is the present definition being widened?
Yes>. I have not the exact citation, but I think a decision was made by one of the courts throwing some doubts on whether " structure " included power lines and that kind of thing.
What is an " aboiteau?" I know it was a work well known to the Acadian farmers of the old days.
I think it means dyke.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is a very well known term in the country from which I come. It means the embankment which is made across a creek running into a piece of land that has been dyked off from the sea. There are creeks in such land, and it is necessary to build a very much heavier embankment than usual across such creeks, and they are called aboiteaux. Usually there is a sluiceway through which the water can enter to a limited extent into the creek. One supposed derivation of the word is from the two words " abattre " and " eau."

The whole question arises over the uncertainty as to whether the former Act covered overhead cables and wires of different kinds. The idea of this Bill is to follow the lines of the Railway Act, which prevents telephone, telegraph, electric light and power companies from stringing wires over a railway except under special plans and specifications approved by the Railway Board. The idea is that this was to be the same thing, except it was to be approved by the Minister of Public Works.

Applications have been
made when wires were stretched over the St. Lawrence.

I dare say; I have not
the exact citation here, but I know some of the courts have questioned whether the word "work," as defined in the original Act, was broad enough to cover this particular kind of structure. To take it out of iany controversy it has been suggested by the officers of the department, and I think, rightly so, that this small amending Act should be passed. That is practically the only object of the Bill. It goes a little further than that however, and there is another phase of it. I refer to sections 4 and 5. The original Act provided that no work should be placed upon or built over or crossing a navigable stream except on plans approved by the Governor in Council, bui this did not apply to small wharves, or small protections where the cost did not exceed $1,000. The language of section 4 is obscure and it is intended to make it perfectly plain that there can be no quesr tion that it must have the consent of the Minister of Public Works. Section 5 which is an extension of the former section, provides that if any works are constructed in, upon or along a navigable stream without the consent of the proper authorities they may be removed by an Order in Council. This goes further and provides that whatever salvage there is may be sold and credited up to the cost, and the owner can be compelled to supply the deficiency whatever that may be. That seems to me to he logical. If there be an" authority in the country which has the right to say what obstructions there shall toe to navigation, whether or not anything shall be built, in or upon or along a navigable stream, then if any person chooses to build any of these erections without the consent of the proper authorities he ought not to find very much fault with their removal. I think those are really the principal objects of the Bill.

There is another change, if I' remember. Under the old Act the Governor in Council, or the Minister of Public Works, had the right to order the destruction of the works if they were an obstruction to navigation. Under this Bill the right is absolute. I think the Act is all right, and I perfectly agree with the Minister of Public Works that these various works which were not completed at the time of the passing of the first Act, such as running pipes over the river to carry water, running power wires over the St. Lawrence as they do, was not contemplated at the time. But there is one case where a grave injustice is being worked, and I want to call my hon. friend's attention to it, because
the matter has been hanging fire for a long while and I do not think the consent of the Governor in Council ought to be refused. The people of Shawinigan Falls could not cross the river with boats on account of the great quantity of logs which aceummulated there every spring. They got together and asked the provincial government to furnish one fourth of the funds, the municipality one fourth, and the Shawinigan, the Belgo-Canadian, the Electrical Chemical company and all the companies that are using the power,' to furnish the other fourth. These people did not bother about any statute. They went to work and took advantage of the ice, and -started their piers. I asked them one day: " Have you permission of the Public Works?" They said, " Why? We have the permission of the provincial government, which is contributing to this bridge'; and this is their river." I said to them: " The St. Maurice is 'a navigable river." I then made the proper application and prepared the necessary documents. At that time the false works were all up and the ice on the eve of breaking, and if it had broken, the whole structure would have come down, and there would have been a loss of $80,000 or $90,000, or perhaps more. When the advertisements were all complete, and the four weeks were over, I presented my application. Naturally the Justice Department reported that the site must be approved, although the statute said that all works constructed before a certain time shall not require such approval, but we did not come within the exception. But in this ease the Department of Justice were -strictly within the law. I may add en passant that we got a letter from the secretary of the Public Works Department, under the amendment of 1908, which authorized the Governor in Council or Minister of Public Works to tear down this structure, ordering ns so to do. I am not sure as to the date of the amendment ordering the town of Shawinigan Falls to tear down their bridge. They were in an awful state, and I came up to Ottawa about the matter. The St. Maurice is a navigable river and it is a non-navigable river, paradoxical as that may seem. Parts of the river are not navigable. At this particular point it is not navigable, except for the alligator of the Government which runs near the falls to pull the booms in. This boat can pull itself ashore and go around the falls. The injustice is this: the municipality paid its share andi the provincial government paid its share, and the companies say, "You are not in a position to

collect money from us because you are not authorized by the Government, the site has not been approved 'by the Governor in Council." This matter has been hanging fire for four or five years, and I have been trying to have it arranged. I think an exception should be made in this case. The construction was made in good faith. I may say the bridge was being built under the supervision of the engineer of the Public Works Department in Quebec, and if we had stopped when we were told to stop, the whole false work would have gone out and the superstructure would have been carried away.
Has it been completed?
Yes, but there is that part of the money that was promised to the company.
Have you applied to the Public Works Department for a certificate of some kind?

No, they applied for
leave and approval of the plans after the bridge was completed. The bridge had been commenced when it came to the notice of these people that they had no authority. It was commenced in ignorance of the law, and when we gave notice and the application was made, we had to advertise for four weeks. The ice was on the eve of breaking away, and they were ordered to stop, and if we had stopped it would have been a dead loss.
Was it above or below the falls?
Above the falls.
I do not suppose any one can seriously say it interferes with navigation to any considerable extent.
Certainly not.
My hon. friend will see that the amendment proposed in no way changes the previous law.

No, but the provision
may work a 'hardship in cases like this.

I do mot know just
how far the department would be justified in going in order to approve of plans of that kind, but a reasonable amount of common sense should be exercised in such a case, and if the hon. gentleman can convince the present Minister of Public Works that this is not an interference with navigation and that he has the power to ap-

prove.the plans and specifications he will not be long in doing it.

That is the trouble. I
do no't think he has the power to ratify plans under the Act when the work is finished. The Act gives him power to approve of the site and plans. The objection that was taken toy the Deputy Minister of Justice was the fact of the bridge being built, and the site occupied and plans being executed. He had nothing to recommend. It was beyond the power of the minister to do anything. But I will take i't up later on.
" 'Mr. CARVELL: 'I am expressing a very offhand view, tout notwithstanding the very high authority the hon. gentleman quotes it seems to me there should be a large element of common sense in dealing with matters of this kind, and I would be disposed to go the whole limit in order to rectify it.	*

I am glad to hear that.
I will take the matter up with my hon. friend.

Have any applications ever been made to the Department of Public Works by any private interests concerning the project of damming the River St. Lawrence at Long Sault? For many years various attempts have been made by private interests to obtain from the Canadian Government the necessary powers to dam the St. Lawrence at that point. The water-power to be developed at Long Sault is one of the most important, if not the most important, after Niagara Falls. There are some gentlemen in the United States and Canada who are banded together in order to force the hand of this Government just as they were banded together to force our hands when we were in office. Fortunately, so far, the Governments which preceded the present one have kept these interests at bay. This syndicate has not been allowed to get control of this magnificent water-power. My hon. friend is aware that there is a strong feeling in the country in favour of the Government owning the remaining water powers on the St. Lawrence. I am not arguing in favour of the Government ownership of railways. I am not discussing that phase of the question of Government ownership, but I am speaking of water-power. Where the Government has the upper hand in reference to this question of water-power it should keep these powers, and if the river is to be harnessed it should toe harnessed as a Government enterprise and for the greatest good to Canadian consumers. With the

scarcity of coal that exists, it is' of the utmost importance that our water-power should he conserved for and in the interest of the public. While I believe in competition in regard to the operation of railways, and while I have yet to learn that government ownership is the best thing in connection with railway operation, I am a believer in government ownership as regards the water-powers of the country, particularly those large water-powers on the St. Lawrence river, and I hope my hon. friend will prove to be the faithful watchdog of the Canadian people.

I am somewhat surprised that my hon. friend digs up the old ghost that I thought had ceased to exist seven or eight years ago. We spent thirty-six or forty-eight hours' time in the old House of Commons debating that question, and I have never heard of it since.
It exists.

Since II assumed the duties of (Minister of Public Works, no application has been made to me either officially or privately and I have never heard the matter discussed, except that I read something in the report of the Conservation Commission which was sent to me a few days ago. The secretary of that commission seemed to be chasing that phantom, the same as my hon. friend is to-night, but. I can assure him that it is only a phantom and no person need lie awake at nights for fear that some of the Dominion's interests are going to be sacrificed by the gobbling up of these water-powers on the St. Lawrence. I had a big flood of telegrams from all sorts and conditions of people,	municipalities	and	organizations, from	the	Atlantic	to	thePacific, in October	last,	protesting against
the ratification of plans farther down the river, I think, somewhere below Beau-harn'ois.
The Cascades?
It was below Beauharn-ois.
The	Cedars?

I think it was below the Cedars, but I never looked into it. I understand that in the month of September somebody gave notice that he would apply to the Public Works Department for the approval of plans but the application has not been made. I can assure my hon. friend he can rest easy and rely upon the old doctrine that sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.

Between the county of Selkirk and the county of Springfield there are a number of ferries crossing the Red river. They are operated by means of cables stretched across the river which can be lowered when a steamboat is approaching or passing. Would they be affected by the operation of this Bill?

Not by any means. The object of this Bill is to see that these ferries shall be installed according to specifications ratified by the department. The chief object of the Bill is to see that no such obstruction as a wire ferry shall be placed across a navigable stream until it has been properly investigated, a proper plan prepared and the work constructed according to this plan.
These ferries have been in operation for a great many years.

There is a provision regarding them in the original Act. I can assure my hon. friend that this Bill is not aimed at anything like that. This Bill is to protect things of that kind, but to see that no obstruction is put across a navigable stream without the matter being properly investigated.
Bill reported read the third time and passed.

On the motion of Hon. F. B. Carvell (Minister of Public Works) the House went into committee on Bill No. 40 to amend the Public Works Act, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Power to dredge, etc., beds of navigable waters.
Does the necessity for this legislation arise owing to a judicial decision?
No, I do not know that it arises over a judicial decision.
It is confiscation of part of the bed of a river.

My hon. friend is right in a sen-se, but I would say that it is expropriation of property rather than confiscation. We have been going on for a great many years, but the only authority which the Government have for taking possession of the beds or 'banks of rivers for the construction of public works has been the vote by Parliament. That is, when the money has been voted for the work it is the only authority we have, and the question has arisen as to whether that is sufficient authority. The officers of the department,
7.34

and contractors and other persons working under them, have been threatened with suits for trespass, and as I hardly know a member of this House who does not want public works in his constituency, I fail to see how I am going to meet all these requests unless I can get authority to go on the land and do what is necessary. It might to some extent amount to what my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) calls confiscation, but if it so be, it is confiscation for the public good. One can hardly imagine the Public Works Department deliberately confiscating property without rendering some value to the community concerned.

In this oase the bed of the river?
Mr. CARVE,LL: The bed of the river or some place along the bank. You must have a place to put your wharf on, or your pier, or things of that kind, and this is really a sort of short-cut, I would say, to the expropriation of the property required. I do not think there is any question whatever but that this Parliament has the jurisdiction.
I do not know about that.

I have not the citation at hand, but I remember a case some years ago in which our good old friend Mr. Con-mee was asking for a charter. The question arose as to the right of the Dominion to expropriate-even the right of the Crown as represented' by a province-and I remember that the decision- of the Privy Council explicitly stated that we had that right. Therefore, I think there is no question about our jurisdiction.
What was that oase?

I have forgotten the
name of the case, it is some eight or nine years since I looked it up, but I am sure there is a decision of the Privy Council to that effect. Therefore, having the jurisdiction, it seems to me very proper that we should have authority, and that is the sole object of this Bill.
Has it not been the practice to purchase land needed by the Public Works Department as the site for a wharf?

I think so, and this Bill does not say that we are going to confiscate ; it only gives us the right to take possession. I cannot conceive that the Government will confiscate people's property, it is only a short cut to expropriation.
[Mr. Carvell 1

My observation in regard to confiscation was said by way of a joke, but I am sorry that my hon- friend the Minister of Public Works did not consult the Attorney General for the various provinces before introducing this legislation. However, it cannot do any harm, (because it is in the public interest and with the object of improving navigation. Referring to the river St. Maurice, part of that river is in the harbour of Three Rivers, and harbours, as hon. gentlemen know, are within the jurisdiction of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The works in that part of the river St. Maurice which is in the harbour of Three Rivers are maintained by the Department of Public Works. On account of a contract made between the St. Maurice Boom and Driving company and the Department of Public Works-^-a contract which I think ought not to have been made, but at any rate it was done- 12 p.m. the department have been paying for all the piers, for the booms and for everything.
New, the Canada Iron Foundries company needed a wharf on which to land pig iron and the clay for their moulds. Application was made to the Department of Public Works, who in turn forwarded it to the Marine Department, and pending the desired permission advantage was taken of the ice by the company to draw materials and go on and complete the work. Now the Department of Marine and Fisheries take the position that parties may not build a dock before getting the approval of the department, whereas the location for the dock has to be approved by the Department of Public Works. We are in this unhappy position, as between the two departments, that we do not know who has jurisdiction, and we .are all at sea.
I am sorry, but they are wonderful people at Three Rivers.
I am not finding fault, but I think the question of jurisdiction ought to be settled.
I know, the people there are willing to accept almost anything. In fact, I understand they want to build ships on dry land and then get the department to dredge a launching basin for them.

Sites have to be got on land, they cannot build them on the water.
. Mr. CARVELL: To go back to the suggestion of my hon. friend as to the booms and piers, I do not think he should object to that. If the Dominion of Canada for forty years have been doing that which they have

no right to do, surely he cannot object to their trying to get back to solid ground and handing those booms and piers over to the people who are using them. I do not want to get into a discussion on the point now, because that raises the question as to the Gatineau river, and I think the Ottawa river also. Why on earth the Dominion of Canada should provide booms and piers for the big lumber corporations is something I could never understand. Furthermore, why Three Rivers, and the Gatineau and Ottawa rivers should be singled out from all the rest of the rivers in Canada is a mystery to me. I think it was a very wise provision indeed to get these particular piers and booms out of the jurisdiction of the Public Works Department, and the Government generally, and let the big corporations look after them the same as is done elsewhere in Canada.

What about compensation for damages if any should arise?
' Mr. CARVELL: I want to point out to my hon. friend that we have been taking this land ever since Confederation. You cannot have public works unless you have the authority to go on the land and construct them. I do not see that there is any change in principle proposed here.
Section approved of, Bill reported and read the third time.
